title: Seeded baton scheduler for structured tasks
description:
## Why

Deliver the next bounded slice of the recorded first demonstration (fx-enq, research/15-rust-dialect.md:237), with the existing language decisions preserved.

- `conformance/README.md (stub oracle limitations)`

## Scope

Depends fx-nkv.3 and fx-nkv.4. The failure-order edge is semantic: the seeded order determines which observed failure wins. Scope: a single runnable task at a time at every scheduling point used by the supported APIs; deterministic seed choice, and wait-state trace records for join and Shared acquisition in this subset. No timers, clocks, files or networking are exposed until their modeled behavior exists.

## Acceptance

a fixed seeded two-task workload has byte-identical decision traces on rerun, distinct seeds cover at least two interleavings, and the trace records each task blocked in join or Shared acquisition with its span. A finite scheduler-internal fixture with two waiters that are never woken reports both as blocked. The user-visible global-deadlock report (03 section 9.3) stays an obligation for the slice exposing channels or limit; do not add those APIs to satisfy this demonstration. This slice owns scheduler policy; capability adapters report checkpoints rather than duplicate scheduling choices.

Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

comments.text: From fx-nkv.4 review (2026-11-10): Shared::with reserves a FIFO ticket and then waits on an OS condvar. Under the baton scheduler, the scheduling point must come before the ticket reservation, or the wait must hand off the baton; otherwise a task descheduled between reserving and acquiring parks later contenders in a wait the baton holder can't satisfy.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: 2026-11-10: Fable research (ufable, owner asked to use Fable for useful Tide work) is preparing options and recommendations for this bead's open design choices, with cited prior art. Report in /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-*/report.md; the coordinator records the decisions here before an implementer starts.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-sched/report.md; the report lands in research/ with this bead). The design fixes engine (baton-passed OS threads), points, strategies and the test surface (03 §9; reference §6.8); these settle the rest:
1. Baton over the existing thread runtime in two layers: a pure decision core with no threads (task states, block(task, wait, span), wake, pick(rng), trace, blocked list) inside the existing Runtime as an optional field (one owner, one lock), and a thin baton (one mutex, one Condvar per task, while current != me). No new dependency.
2. Simulation identity: Tasks carries a private Option<Arc<sim>>; Shared::new copies it into the cell; a handle used across simulations or outside one panics with a clear message. CURRENT stays 'which task am I'.
3. Points: spawn (parent registers the child, starts the thread, takes one point; child first waits for the baton); join (point on entry, block(Join) if unfinished); scope exit (block(ScopeExit) before thread::scope's OS join); Shared::with (point before ticket reservation, existing body, point after release); checkpoint (point then cancel check); yield_now (check, point, check; no thread::yield_now under sim); task finish (record outcome, wake waiters, pick, hand over: last user-visible act, no user Drop after it). Sleep/timers/channels are not in this slice. A point with one runnable task draws nothing and emits no sched event.
4. Shared under sim: the cell is never contended (LOCK-4: Pure closure has no points), so the condvar wait becomes a hard internal panic 'contended cell under the simulator'. Acceptance reading (recorded here as a technical reading, not a weakened check): every point records the task's pending operation as its wait state; a join wait is 'blocked', a cell wait is 'ready at cell(id)'; the internal fixture exercises block() directly with two never-woken waiters of each kind.
5. Strategy: uniform random among runnable tasks (current included) at every point with >1 runnable; fifo only if a test needs it; no PCT (not v0). Per-seed owned SplitMix64; scheduler stream derived from the seed with a fixed domain constant so later draws (fx-o8j, fx-byk.2) get their own streams; index drawn from u64, never usize.
6. Determinism: decisions depend only on seed and runnable sets ordered by task id; task/scope/cell ids are simulation-local counters (LOCK-3's 'deterministic under the simulator'; fx-ugm must use them too); spans via #[track_caller] Location::caller(); no address, thread id, wall time or hash order in any event. Scheduler state in Vec/BTreeMap.
7. Panics: the baton hand-off happens in run's existing catch_unwind path, not in a destructor; scheduler-lock poison is fatal for the seed.

traces/output, and the runner reports the seed and exits nonzero on failure. This is a real
scheduler-found bug, not a canned injected error. A `#[sim_test(seeds = 20)]` test and a plain

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-sched/report.md; see also fx-nkv.5's comment of the same date):
1. Trace: NDJSON, one event per line, hand-written with fixed key order, no serializer dependency; kinds in this slice sched (step, sorted runnable ids, chosen), spawn, exit, cancel, cell (acquire/release, id), join and scope_exit wait/wake, sink (stream, message); each event has step, task, kind, operation, span, wait state. Field names stay provisional until fx-nkv.7.
2. Replay = rerun the seed (record no schedule). Self-check compares the two traces byte for byte and prints the first differing line pair; trace_hash waits for fx-nkv.7.
3. Root::sim(seed): calling thread becomes task 0 holding the baton; dropping SimRoot ends the simulation (assert no live task); in-process for plain #[test].
4. #[sim_test(seeds = N)]: expands to a parameterless #[test] calling one hidden std entry; parent re-executes current_exe with --exact <path> --nocapture and a private env var, stdin closed, wall-clock timeout; child runs seeds 0..N in order with a fresh SimRoot each, prints one line per seed start, catches panics per seed, runs the first and any failing seed twice for the self-check, prints seed/failure/trace and exits nonzero. Abort or timeout is attributed to the last started seed. One child per test.
5. seeds = N means 0..N. A single seed is selected through a toolchain-internal env var (the hook a later tide test --seed and fx-nkv.8's one command call).
6. Under simulation sinks append sink events and don't write to real stdout; the runner prints a failing seed's records. 'Output' in identity checks = ordered sink events.
7. No step limit in this slice; the runner timeout is the backstop.

comments.text: Research started 2026-11-12 (coordinator): Sol (gpt-6.1-sol, high) drafts options + recommendations in pane p72; brief /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-replay/brief.md, report report.md in the same directory. The coordinator (Opus) then records the design decisions here.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-12 (coordinator Opus, from Sol research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-replay/report.md; it lands in research/ as 28-replay-manifests.md with this bead): adopt the report's recommendations 1-7, with these bindings.
1. Owners: the driver owns build identity (a receipt paired with the executable); the trusted std harness writes the run manifest; the macro supplies test source/origin. Versioned JSON 'tide-replay/1', trace bytes inline, initial manifest written before user evaluation and atomically replaced; exclusive-create names (test, seed, evaluation ordinal, build id); never overwrite another run.
2. Semantic identity = a structured receipt: admitted and paired-library source maps (logical relative names + exact snapshot bytes), artifact content hashes for supplied std/macros/dependency dirs (called artifact hashes, not source provenance), compiler -vV, target, profile, effective semantic options with physical paths replaced by roles, tide-admit/tide-std/tide-macros identity, generator and trace format versions. Computed once from the same snapshot that compiled (both compile_with_library snapshots), recomputed before replay even on a cache hit. Not the existing cache key (it holds absolute paths). Same-machine replay with identical pinned artifacts is the promise; cross-machine replay is not promised.
3. Inputs: seed plus a versioned typed choice tape actually consumed (lossless integers, kinds/bounds), the derivation version of fx-m72.2's parameter stream and the scheduler stream, effective config, ordered Root::sim ordinals. No Serialize bound on parameters. Replay consumes the tape strictly (exhaustion, leftovers, bad kinds fail); no shrinking or generation on replay; no config overrides.
4. Command: a labelled partial precursor 'tide-admit --replay <manifest>' with its existing explicit source/build arguments; validation (version, digests, current snapshot vs receipt, executable vs receipt) finishes before any candidate process starts; no force option; diagnostics name the mismatched component and suggest a fresh --seed run. Fresh --seed on the same path; the two modes are mutually exclusive. Print the real shell-quoted invocation on failure; relabel existing seed hints as fresh reruns.
5. Proof: compare each replay's exact NDJSON trace bytes (SHA-256 + first difference) and stable outcome signature with the original recording, and the two replays with each other; exclude libtest/progress output, wall time and PIDs. One manifest = one evaluation; a printed minimized artifact gets its own re-evaluated trace.
6. Task-0 span: pass the macro's Config.call Source into the hidden simulator construction; public Root::sim keeps #[track_caller].
7. Runtime children get a cleared environment plus explicit harness controls. Out of scope: fault plans, durability, crash models, external injected inputs (none exist in this slice), signing.

Verification is fx-nkv's full acceptance, from clean checkout with pinned tools; the guide distinguishes runnable support from future v0 features. This closes the application/documentation gap without growing the 25k core reference. This is demonstration evidence only; E3's paired planted-change study remains distinct.

## Acceptance

From a clean checkout with pinned tools, the planned demo/run.sh exits 0 and demonstrates fx-nkv acceptance: a scheduling-dependent failing seed, two identical replay traces, a fixed revision passing an explicit seed set, and an authority-widening diff on the same service. The runnable human guide and concise agent card describe only implemented support.

title: Define the minimal Ferox v1 package manifest and workspace-loading contract for bootstrap check/fmt flows
description: The spec now defines ferox.toml, workspace manifests, package-loading facts, and deterministic machine-readable metadata, but the bootstrap queue does not yet track the minimal contract needed to make early ferox check and ferox fmt flows honest. This task should define the smallest package/workspace-loading surface the Rust bootstrap must implement, what can stay stubbed, and how CLI/output behavior should expose package-loading and manifest facts without overbuilding the package system.
design: Primary question: what minimal manifest and workspace-loading contract is required for the first real bootstrap CLI flows? Define: 1. the smallest ferox.toml and workspace manifest subset needed for single-package and workspace-local flows; 2. how package loading, workspace member discovery, and target selection should behave in v1 bootstrap; 3. what machine-readable metadata and failure facts must be exposed; 4. what registry, publishing, and advanced dependency features remain intentionally out of scope.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what manifest fields and workspace rules are required for bootstrap; what package-loading behavior ferox check/fmt must support; what machine-readable package/workspace facts are emitted; and what package-system features remain deferred. Include one worked single-package example, one worked workspace example, validation expectations for pass/fail manifest fixtures, and logging expectations for manifest parsing, workspace discovery, and package-loading diagnostics.
notes: Decision: the first bootstrap package/workspace-loading layer should support local package roots, explicit workspace member lists, conventional or explicit lib/bin targets, local path dependencies, and deterministic machine-readable package-loading facts. Registry fetching, alternate sources, feature flags, and advanced dependency modes stay out of the first real check/fmt flows and must fail explicitly if encountered.

title: Decide: stop agents asking the owner technical questions
description:
## Why

Agents keep handing the owner technical choices: option menus, "yours to make", and "want me to file beads?". The owner answers with "do what you think is better", "i trust your judgment", or "you make the decisions". This continued at least twice after the Decisions rule landed in AGENTS.md (04302c9, 2026-10-20). Every such question stalls the run until the owner replies.

## Evidence

Owner corrections (session prefix, UTC date, quote):
- 3748816d, 2026-10-19: "2. do what you think is better"; "i will trust your research"
- 0c465b0b, 2026-10-19: a three-way menu on AI_SUPERVISOR.md, answered "do it"
- 9cc7dc47, 2026-10-20: "dont ask me tecnical questions", the answer to a question about io::Error's Pure bound (recorded in the `no-technical-questions` memory)
- 3536eb7f, 2026-10-20, after the rule: the agent called raising the 25k budget "a scope call and yours to make"; the owner said "you make the decisions, i just help here and there"
- c697036a, 2026-10-21, after the rule and the memory: "Should I add 3 to that change?", answered "ok i trust your judgment"
- The same pattern for follow-up beads: 186ae567 "file them", 182a586e "yeah, and continue", f54f050d and 9cc7dc47 "yeah"

Current owners and why they failed:
- AGENTS.md "Decisions" (local overlay): it separates scope from technical choices, but the agent keeps labelling budgets, thresholds, governance mechanics, and follow-up beads as scope. Ambiguous.
- AP-PLAN-001 (canonical): "Report unapproved findings; create issues only for material out-of-scope or schedulable work, deferred outside authorized batches". Agents read this as needing approval before filing follow-ups (186ae567: "this run owned only fx-pcb, so I haven't created them"). Ambiguous. That fix belongs in the Starcompass source repository and is reported, not filed, here.
- AP-SCOPE-001 "stop when a missing scope choice would materially change the result" pulls toward asking. Nothing local says which way an unclear case should go.
- User memory `no-technical-questions`: wording only, and it lives only on this machine.

## Scope

In scope:
- `.claude/settings.json` (permissions)
- the Decisions section in `.agent-protocols.local.md`, with a re-render of `AGENTS.md`

Out of scope:
- canonical protocol text (AP-PLAN-001, AP-SCOPE-001)
- the owner's real scope calls: new features, priorities, publishing, repository moves

## Acceptance

- The AskUserQuestion tool is unavailable in this project.
- In a behavior trial with no expected answer given, a fresh agent faces the three recorded cases (the 25k→30k budget, adding a governance change to a pending commit, filing two follow-up beads). It decides each one, records it, and reports it without asking.
- A control case (whether to publish the repository to a collaborator) is still asked, because it is a scope call.

## Implementation Notes

Recommended enforcement, highest that works:
1. Structure: deny `AskUserQuestion` in the project's `.claude/settings.json` permissions. That removes the menu path entirely. The owner's earlier correction answered such a menu.
2. Behavior-trialled wording: add one line to Decisions that classifies the recurring cases. Budgets, thresholds, review mechanics, and filing follow-up beads are the agent's. When a case is unclear, the agent decides, records it, and reports it. Then run the trial in Acceptance (AP-TEST-001).

Rejected:
- A Stop hook that flags messages ending in "?": it blocks real scope questions and conversational answers.
- Wording without a trial: that is the state today, and it failed twice.

## Verification

- `claude -p` in this repository cannot call AskUserQuestion (it is denied by settings).
- The behavior trial above, run by a fresh subagent, with its transcript summarized on this bead.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the owner wants to keep AskUserQuestion for scope questions. Then do only step 2.
- Stop if the trial still asks on the recorded cases after two wordings that use different mechanisms.

## Maintenance Notes

- To report to Starcompass if the owner asks: AP-PLAN-001 should say whether a run may file follow-up issues for material findings without per-issue approval.

title: Decide File::close(self) under cancellation (TASK-3 consuming checkpoint)
description:
## Why

`File::close(self) -> io::Result<()>` consumes the `File`, and every `File` operation suspends and
so is a cancellation checkpoint (03 §1.1). TASK-3 requires an operation that consumes a value to
return it inside its cancellation error, and an `io::Error` cannot hold a `File`. TASK-6 says
cleanup I/O is "an explicit `close(self)` called under `shield`", but nothing says what an
unshielded `close` in a cancelled scope does. fx-obr fixed the same conflict for
`Child::wait_with_output` by taking `&mut self` (round 70 B1); `close` needs its own decision.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 `File` row (Suspends: all) and Receivers note
  (`File::close` takes `self`); TASK-3; TASK-6.
- `design/reference.md` 6.3 (`fn close(self) -> io::Result<()>`), 7.2.
- `reviews/round70-codex.md` B1 (the `wait_with_output` case).

## Scope

In scope: decide `close`'s behavior under cancellation (for example: `close` is not a checkpoint
and always completes; or it closes the descriptor and reports cancellation; or another receiver or
error shape), and check every other handle for a consuming checkpoint method. State it in 03 and
the reference pair.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides it with reasoning, consistent with TASK-3 and TASK-6; the reference pair states it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge. The core reference is at 24,993 of 25,000 tokens.
close_reason: File::close is shielded (03 §1.1, TASK-3/5/6, core 7.2); core 24,999 tokens; rounds 73-75 clean (Codex approve, round 75)

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decision (03 §0, §1.1 File row and Receivers note, TASK-3, TASK-5, TASK-6; core 7.2): File::close(self) is shielded: it may suspend but is not a checkpoint, always closes the descriptor and returns the close's own result even in a cancelled scope. Reasons: reporting close's result is its only purpose beyond drop; returning Cancelled would lose it; returning the File in the error needs a non-io::Error type and leaves a retry that fails again under level-triggered cancellation unless run under shield. Cost: like drop it cannot be interrupted (TASK-5 names it; NFS can block it). Rejected: close-then-report-Cancelled; a dedicated error carrying File.
Handle sweep (round 73): no other handle has a consuming checkpoint; BufWriter::into_inner already returns the writer; wait_with_output was fixed by fx-obr.
Not applied: round 73 N2 (01 D8's approximate wording; 03 §0 owns the exception) and N4 (core 7.2 literal reading; core at 24,999 of 25,000 tokens).

title: Channels with cancellation-aware errors
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P4, and no existing bead owns it.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P4, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §7.3; design/03-authority-concurrency.md channel rules`

## Scope

channel(tasks), sync_channel(n, tasks), Sender clone, send, try_send, recv, try_recv, recv_deadline, iteration, and the RecvError/RecvTimeoutError/SendError enums with is_cancelled(), real and simulated, including the global-deadlock report for blocked channel waits. language semantics.

## Acceptance

Bounded sends block at capacity as checkpoints; a disconnect ends iteration; recv in a cancelled scope returns the Cancelled variant; a simulated run whose tasks all wait on channels reports a deadlock. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-chan/report.md §§1.1-1.8 and §4 items 1-4; the report lands in research/ as 21-channels-tcp.md with fx-o4h): adopt the report's recommendations.
1. Checkpoints: recv, recv_deadline and SyncSender::send check cancellation on entry whatever the channel holds; a cancelled recv leaves a buffered message in place (Trio's property). Sender::send, try_send, try_recv, clone, drop are not checkpoints. After a wait: receiver order cancellation > message > Disconnected > Timeout; a blocked sender whose value was taken returns Ok(()), else removes its entry and returns Cancelled(v)/Disconnected(v).
2. Owned queue, no dependency (std mpsc and crossbeam-channel rejected: a blocked op can't be woken by cancellation or return its value, and holds the baton). One Arc<Chan<T>> mutex over buffer, pending (ticket, value) senders in arrival order, one blocked receiver; no barging; rendezvous send returns only after a recv took the value; try_send on n==0 succeeds only with a blocked receiver.
3. Waits use the runtime's one wait primitive (wait(kind, span, until, cancellable)) that fx-o8j/fx-zc1's decisions define; this bead adds wait kinds recv(chan)/send(chan) and no cancellation logic of its own. Real side: park_timeout loop rechecking under the lock; lock order channel then runtime. Sim: one point on entry (before looking at the channel), then the cancel check, then act or block; try_ forms are points; creation and drop are not; mutex never held across a point; sim identity and simulation-local id from Tasks.
4. Disconnect/drop: Rust's rules; receiver drop wakes blocked senders with Disconnected(v) and drops buffered values after releasing the lock; drop never blocks, is no point, records a close event, is unwind-safe; no echo bit.
5. recv_deadline = recv with until (sim timer, real park_timeout); a ready message is returned even past the deadline (§4 item 4); past deadline + empty -> Timeout without blocking.
6. Iteration: iter/IntoIterator/try_iter, each next() one recv().ok() (checkpoint and point).
7. No own deadlock detector: channel waits are blocks named recv/send(chan) in the shared deadlock report (whichever of fx-zc1/fx-o4h lands first builds it). Trace kind chan: new, send/try_send, recv/try_recv/recv_deadline, close; never the payload.
Record §4 items 1-3 in design/03 §6.4.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Lock order (2026-11-11, coordinator Opus, from fx-o8j round-1 Opus review finding 2): the shared wait primitive (fx-o8j, Context::wait) takes the runtime lock, then the resource lock. A channel keeps its own waiter Thread handles and never takes the runtime lock while holding its own lock. This replaces decision 3's 'channel then runtime', which with fx-o8j's order would deadlock (ABBA) on the real side. Readiness is a caller-supplied check, or the resource tracks its own waiters; Runtime::wait_done sees only Runtime state.

title: Clock, Instant, and virtual time
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P2, and no existing bead owns it. fx-o8o's map:
B10 fails on E0432 for task::Cancelled and time::Duration, C5 on time::Duration.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P2, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §6.1, §6.8, §7.2, §12.3; design/01-design.md D15`

## Scope

Clock (now, system_time, sleep, sleep_until, monotonic_only); std::time's Duration (Rust's), Instant
(a distinct type with no now() or elapsed(), 03 CAP-1, otherwise Rust's API, as the conformance stub
declares) and SystemTime, with their arithmetic; std::task::Cancelled (Debug, Clone, Copy,
PartialEq, Eq, Error, Pure), the error sleep and sleep_until return, which fx-zc1's checkpoint and
later checkpoints reuse; real implementations, and simulated virtual time that advances only when
every task is blocked, with sim.elapsed(). Production std under crates/, built and admitted through
tide-admit; no new language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply.

## Acceptance

A sleeping task under the simulator wakes at the exact virtual instant and sim.elapsed() reports it;
real sleeps take at least their duration; sleep in a cancelled scope returns Cancelled; E1 task B10
no longer fails on task::Cancelled or time::Duration. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not
only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the
production library owns runtime behavior.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-time/report.md §§1.1-1.4, 1.9, §4; the report lands in research/ as 20-time.md with fx-o8j): adopt the report's recommendations.
1. Representation (report option A, matching the stub): Instant as an offset from a process anchor on the real side and virtual now under the simulator, one Debug form, one arithmetic path, no brand; Rust's arithmetic exactly (Add/Sub Duration panic on overflow with checked_*; duration_since/Sub<Instant> saturate; SystemTime from UNIX_EPOCH with Result duration_since); Instant has Rust's method set minus now/elapsed.
2. Virtual time advances only in fx-nkv.5's decision core: in pick(), if nothing is runnable, set now to the earliest deadline, fire every timer at that instant, pick among the woken; if no timer, global deadlock report. No tick or epsilon. now stored as Duration; sim.elapsed() returns it. fx-o8j draws no random numbers.
3. Timers: BTreeMap keyed (deadline, class, id): class 0 scope deadlines (scope id; parents first), class 1 operation timers (simulation-local seq). All timers of an instant fire in key order before any task runs. Remove a scope's timer at exit and when set_deadline lowers it.
4. sleep(d) = sleep_until(now.checked_add(d)), overflow = never (no panic). Inside: cancel check; target not after now -> one point, cancel check, return; else register timer, block wait sleep(until), on wake cancel check first. Real side loops on timed park until the target.
5. monotonic_only(): system_time() on it panics naming the attenuation (§4 item 1; record in 03 §1.1). reference §7.2's 'likewise' read as 'takes an Instant from a Clock'.
6. Trace events per the report's §1.9 table (cap clock.now/system_time; sleep with until, wait, result; advance). Deadlock: report the blocked list as the last sched event, then the process exits nonzero (§4 item 7). A yield-loop guard is a simulator diagnostic (§4 item 8).
The shared wait primitive is fx-zc1's (see its comment); if fx-o8j lands first it builds it there with the same shape.

title: E1 harness, acceptance suites, and reference solutions
description:
## Why

fx-ic2 (run E1 on the checked toolchain) waits on 21 prerequisite beads. The trial's own
machinery, `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §6 (acceptance suites, structure checks, reference
solutions) and the render script and `./check` wrapper that §4 and §5 describe, does not depend on
them, and writing it early shows which tasks still lack an executable surface while the
prerequisites are open. Owner decision, 2026-11-01 (recommended by fx-gfq's worker, approved by
the owner in session): file it as a separate, unblocked bead.

## Scope

For all 30 tasks in `trials/e1-checked/tasks.md`: the Rust arm's acceptance suites, structure
checks, and reference solutions, run green on the recorded Rust toolchain; the Tide arm's suites,
structure checks, and reference solutions written against the protocol's API, each run as far as
the current checked toolchain allows, with every failure mapped to the §10.1 prerequisite bead
that owns it; and the render script and `./check` wrapper. Keep everything outside any writer's
directory (§2's held-out rules). Do not freeze the suites; §6's freeze and its SHA-256 belong to
fx-ic2, before the first gate session. No protocol, task, or threshold changes; a problem found in
the frozen protocol goes on fx-ic2 as a comment.

## Acceptance

Every Rust-arm reference solution passes `./check`, its structure check, and its acceptance suite
on the recorded toolchain. Every Tide-arm reference solution either does the same on the checked
toolchain or has its failure mapped, on this bead, to an open §10.1 prerequisite bead that blocks
fx-ic2. A missing owner gets a new prerequisite bead linked to fx-ic2.

Bind /usr read-only as a whole (with /lib and /lib64 as their usr symlinks), plus the minimal Nix store closure Codex computes; drop the per-binary picks from /usr/bin. Reason: per-file mounts failed three times on this host: the Nix interpreter, then GCC's liblto_plugin/collect2, then the target-prefixed x86_64-linux-gnu-ld that collect2 execs, which is the middle link of ld -> x86_64-linux-gnu-ld -> x86_64-linux-gnu-ld.bfd. comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Opus decision (2026-11-07, claude-opus-5-5) on the draft's open choices:

# fx-o8o: Opus decisions on the E1 checked-arm harness draft

Decider: Opus (claude-opus-5-5), 2026-11-07. Candidate: commit `2e158b0` on
branch `fx-o8o`, on `3fdc020`. Scratch, never committed.

Facts checked for these decisions, beyond the report:

- `git diff d944329 2e158b0 -- trials/` is empty, so the rebase left the
  harness tree unchanged. The host-verified Rust proof (30/30 sandboxed,
  harness_test 9/9) covers this tree on the same 1.96.0 toolchain. It goes
  stale with the changes below.
- fx-kw8.9 is **closed** (landed `6748d7c`). The driver now accepts
  `--emit=link` with `--crate-type=bin` (writes `<out>/<name>`) or `--test`
  (writes `<out>/<name>-test`, Rust's ordinary libtest harness for
  parameterless `#[test]`). `--emit=link --crate-type=lib` is refused
  (`invocation.rs:167`), and there is no `--extern`: the only dependency
  inputs are the trusted operator flags `--tide-std` and `--tide-dep-dir`
  (`invocation.rs:125-154`). The draft still hard-codes "awaits fx-kw8.9"
  (`harness.py:202`, `:251`), and `readiness.md` still names fx-kw8.9 as
  the common blocker and as the only owner for A2/A3/A4/A10.
- Every other bead in the readiness map is open and blocks fx-ic2 directly
  (`br show fx-ic2`).
- `cargo +1.96.0 vendor --locked --offline` from this host's registry cache
  reproduces `trials/e1-checked/rust/vendor` **byte for byte**
  (`diff -r` is empty, `.cargo-checksum.json` files included), and leaves
  `Cargo.lock` unchanged. `~/.cargo/registry/cache` holds all 13 locked
  versions. Appending one line to a vendored file makes
  `cargo check --offline --locked` fail with a checksum mismatch, so Cargo
  verifies vendored bytes on every build.
- The pinned 1.96.0 rustdoc contains `RUSTDOC_DOCTEST_BIN_PATH`,
  `RUSTDOC_DOCTEST_RUN_NB_TEST`, the `libdoctest_bundle_` prefix, and the
  attribute `standalone_crate`, but no `standalone`. The adapter relies on
  exactly those names (`doctest-runner.sh:14-24`). The fixture's
  ```` ```standalone ```` block is an unknown fence tag, so rustdoc does
  not treat it as Rust and never runs it.
- `prepare` writes executable `check` and `test` scripts into the
  writer-writable directory (`harness.py:290-293`), and `references` runs
  those files (`harness.py:404`). `command()` runs on the host, outside
  the jail; only its build and test children are jailed.
- `/nix/store` contains no store path whose name matches `tide` or
  `e1-checked`, and the repository has no `*.nix` file. `/usr/local` holds
  nothing private.

## Decisions

### 1. Sandbox backend: Bubblewrap (as drafted)

Decision: keep the fail-closed Bubblewrap backend in `sandbox_command`.

Reasons. §10.3 asks for an operating-system sandbox with five properties:
the fresh copy as the only writable tree; reads limited to the toolchains,
the vendored crates and system files; no network beyond the sandbox's own
loopback; a clean environment; time limits. The draft meets each one:
- `--unshare-all` gives a new network namespace with only loopback, and
  C10 passes inside it on this host;
- one `--bind` for the work tree, and read-only binds only for `/usr`,
  `/etc/alternatives`, `/nix/store`, the sysroot, the vendor tree, the
  doctest wrapper and the Tide artifacts (pinned by the boundary test);
- `environment()` and the driver's own `env_clear`;
- `--die-with-parent`, plus `killpg` on timeout.

Writer code is non-adversarial, measured model output on a single-user
host with no secrets mounted, so kernel-escape resistance buys nothing the
protocol asks for. Bubblewrap 0.12.0 is already installed, adds no
dependency to the repository, and its whole policy is one function, so
replacing it is cheap. Setup failure fails the run, and the only unjailed
mode is `references --local`, for reference sources only.

Rejected: a VM backend (QEMU or Firecracker). It needs a new dependency
plus image provenance, boot time or snapshot-copy machinery, and slower
cargo builds charged to the writers' 40-minute budget. All that buys
isolation the threat model does not need.

Condition, owned by fx-ic2 (§10.2 item 5): before the first writer, run
canaries on the gate host and record them. Jailed code must fail to:
- read `/home`, the repository root, another session or a suite;
- connect to a non-loopback address;
- see an inherited environment variable;
- write outside its work tree.
Also confirm that no `/nix/store` path is a copy of the repository, and
record the bwrap version with the toolchain identities.

### 2. Unavailable Tide execution: driver-only, with no rustc fallback (as drafted), but the adapter now runs what fx-kw8.9 provides

Decision: Tide code builds and links only through `tide-admit` with the
production std. There is no direct-rustc, stub or attribute-stripping
fallback. Protocol §5 says so outright ("Tide code builds only through the
driver; no step falls back to stable rustc or the conformance stub"), and
so does §10.2 item 2 ("through the driver with the production std, never
the stub").

fx-kw8.9 has landed, so the hard-coded "adapter awaits fx-kw8.9" results
must go. The adapter now builds through `--emit=link` and runs:
- writer tests and library acceptance tests through the linked
  `solution-test` harness, with the same per-test 10 s limit and
  completed-result check as Rust;
- binary cases through the linked `solution` binary.

A plain libtest harness is not `tide test`: it has no property tests, no
simulation, no generated contract tests and no vacuity floor. So Tide
writer-test mode keeps an explicit failing result naming fx-nkv.6 and
fx-m72 until their runner exists. A linked or passing plain harness can
never count as complete Tide `./test`. Simulated suites fail by themselves
until `#[sim_test]` exists (fx-nkv.5/fx-nkv.6).

Rejected: a direct-rustc or stub fallback, which the protocol forbids. Also
rejected: keeping the hard-coded failure, because the Acceptance asks for
the Tide arm to run "as far as the current checked toolchain allows", and
for each failure to map to an *open* bead.

### 3. Tide library boundary: a separately admitted crate that imports the candidate; the sibling module stays a probe only

Decision: for a Tide library, readiness and the first-check measure
(§7.1) need the acceptance suite compiled as its own admitted crate that
imports the admitted candidate library. The sibling-module probe
(`mod solution;` plus `#[cfg(test)] mod acceptance;`) stays, so its
execution results are recorded. Every Tide library record also carries an
explicit failing "library boundary" result, so `passed` stays false until
the driver has the interface.

Reasons. The preface tells writers that acceptance tests "are a separate
test file that calls your public items, so every item the task names must
be `pub`". The Rust arm meets that with `tests/acceptance.rs`, a separate
crate. A sibling module also sees `pub(crate)` and `pub(super)` items, and
both are legal Tide (D1 lists `pub(crate)`). So the probe would pass a Tide
writer whom the same code in Rust would fail. §11 allows only asymmetries
that make the Tide arm's job no easier, and this one makes it easier.

The driver cannot build this today. It refuses `--emit=link` for a lib,
and `--tide-dep-dir` is for trusted operator artifacts, so passing a
candidate through it would trust unreviewed code. No open bead owns the
interface: fx-kw8.9 delivered bins and test harnesses only, and fx-nkv.6
and fx-m72 cover runners. The Acceptance says what to do with that: "A
missing owner gets a new prerequisite bead linked to fx-ic2."

Rejected:
- accepting the sibling module as final, which gives the asymmetry above;
- a structure check against restricted visibility, which adds a
  requirement the task text does not state (§6: "exactly what the task's
  checked cases say and nothing more");
- splicing the suite into the candidate crate, which is the same in-crate
  visibility;
- passing the candidate through `--tide-dep-dir`, which trusts unreviewed
  code.

### 4. Rust doctests: keep the pinned per-case adapter (as drafted); fix its fixture

Decision: keep `doctest-runner.sh`. §4.1 gives every test, and `cargo test`
runs doctests, a 10-second wall limit. Edition 2024 merges doctests into
one process, so one timeout per merged executable would fail two
legitimate 6-second doctests together. The adapter drives the pinned
runner's own case-selection protocol (names confirmed in the 1.96.0
rustdoc binary above), uses no unstable flags, and does not rewrite
source. Revalidate it whenever the Rust-arm pin changes; `readiness.md`
already says so.

The self-test's standalone case is broken: rustdoc's attribute is
`standalone_crate`, so the ```` ```standalone ```` block never runs. Fix
the fixture and prove the standalone case ran.

Rejected:
- one timeout per merged binary, which breaks the per-test limit;
- `--merge-doctests=no`, unstable on 1.96.0 and a change to how the
  writer's tests build;
- libtest `--ensure-time`, which reports but does not kill.

### 5. Writer command boundary: trusted dispatch only, with no executable wrapper in the writer directory (changes the draft)

Decision: the writer's `./check` and `./test` are logical commands. The
operator's broker (fx-ic2) maps them to
`python3 <repo>/trials/e1-checked/harness.py command SESSION check|test`.
The harness puts **no** `check` or `test` file in the writer directory,
and nothing ever executes a file from that directory outside the jail.

Answer to the validity question: **yes, under the draft a writer could
fake a pass.** The wrapper is a writer-editable file in a writer-writable
directory; `chmod` is no defence, since the writer can delete and recreate
it. Any runner that executes it, as `references` does today and as a naive
`Bash(./check)` allowlist would, runs the writer's bytes on the host, as
the operator, outside Bubblewrap. That breaks five things:
- §3 isolation: network, `/home`, the repository's held-out suites and
  reference solutions all become readable;
- the §4.2 budget, since such runs are not counted;
- the §7.1 first snapshot, since none is saved;
- the §7.3 iteration count;
- what the writer sees, since a fake green replaces the real verdict.

Final grading re-runs everything from saved snapshots, so a faked
`./check` alone cannot forge the final pass. Everything else above breaks.
The README's warning is not enough, because the draft itself breaks that
rule. Removing the file closes the hole by construction. The preface and
protocol name `./check` and `./test` as commands, so nothing in the frozen
text changes.

Rejected:
- writer-directory scripts executed by the broker (the hazard above);
- read-only scripts (the parent directory is writable);
- running `command()` itself inside the jail. It needs the session state
  and snapshot directory, which must stay out of the writer's reach, and
  its own inputs are trusted.

### 6. Dependency gate (AP-DEPENDENCY-001): option (b), vendor at setup from the pinned `Cargo.lock` (changes the draft)

Decision: delete `trials/e1-checked/rust/vendor/` from the commit. Keep
`rust/Cargo.toml` and `rust/Cargo.lock`, whose `checksum` fields are the
SHA-256 of each `.crate`. A trusted setup step on the host runs
`cargo vendor --locked --offline` from that lockfile into a git-ignored
directory under `target/e1-checked/`. Every jailed build reads that
directory read-only and offline.

Capability and contract: the Rust arm's three permitted crates (serde
1.0.229 with `derive`, serde_json 1.0.154, thiserror 2.0.21) and their 10
transitive crates, at the locked versions, available offline inside the
jail. What the protocol requires:
- §5: "offline, with `serde` … and their lockfile, vendored";
- §10.3: read access to "the recorded toolchains and vendored crates";
- §2's held-out rules, which do not concern third-party crates.
It asks for a vendored, offline, recorded source at build time. It does
not ask for third-party source checked into this repository. (b) gives the
same vendor directory and the same offline jailed builds.

Reproducibility is proven, not assumed. The offline `cargo vendor` from
this host's cache is byte-identical to the committed tree. Cargo checks the
`.crate` archives against the lockfile checksums when it fetches them, and
rejects a vendored file whose bytes changed on every `--locked` build
(tampering test above). crates.io never deletes a published version, and
yanking does not block a locked build. The dependency identity to record
for §5 is the SHA-256 of `Cargo.lock`.

Cost of (a): 597 files, 7.9 MB and about 170k of the commit's 180k lines
are third-party code that no reviewer reads. Every GOVERNANCE review round
pays for it now, and every clone pays for it forever. The repository
vendors nothing else; its own workspace builds offline from the registry.

Rejected:

title: Define the transition from ordinary Ferox to optional contracts, ghost code, and deeper verification
description: Ferox has a promising long-term verification direction, but the transition point is still vague. This task is to define how Ferox should move from the safe core to optional verification layers: what the first contract/spec features should be, how ghost/spec code should remain narrow, how verification should interact with ownership and tooling, and how to prevent the language from drifting into proof-first everyday programming.
design:
Primary question: How should Ferox grow from a safe core into optional verification without turning everyday programming into proof engineering?

Define the transition as a staged gradient:
1. First verification layer: contracts, invariants, pure spec functions, ghost code.
2. Interaction with ownership, checked IR, diagnostics, and tooling.
3. Erasure and runtime model boundaries.
4. Non-goals: what deeper proof features stay out of the core language.

The result should explain where verification begins, what it can prove, and how it stays optional.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What is the first verification layer Ferox should adopt?
- How does that layer interact with ownership and the safe-change tooling contract?
- What stays optional, narrow, and erasable rather than becoming ordinary source-language complexity?
- What verification ambitions are explicitly deferred beyond this layer?

Include:
- one phased roadmap and at least two small examples of the intended contract/spec style;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for contract/spec semantics, pass/fail corpus tests for verified and rejected cases, and end-to-end scripts that exercise mixed ordinary-code plus optional-verification workflows;
- detailed logging/tracing requirements for contract checking, spec/ghost handling, erasure boundaries, and verification-related diagnostics.
notes: Decision: Ferox should grow verification in a staged gradient. V1 remains ordinary code only. The first optional layer is a narrow V2 contract/spec/ghost layer built around requires, ensures, invariants, pure spec functions, and erased ghost code. Stronger proof-oriented constructs remain V3-or-later and should not shape everyday programming unless the narrower layer proves insufficient.

title: Specify resource-handle API surface: Command authority, Child fields under ROOT-4, Stdio
description:
## Why

03 §0 now defines resource handles (fx-zm4), but their API surface is underspecified: the
reference never says a `Command` carries authority, never names `Child`, `Signals`, or `ReadDir`,
and its "every capability method takes `&self`" rule does not fit handles. ROOT-4 says handle
types have no public fields, yet Rust's `Child` exposes `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` as public
fields, and how a `Stdio` built from a `File` is classified is unstated. Found by round 32 (N1,
N2) and round 33 (N3) while reviewing fx-zm4.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §0 (resource-handle list), §1.1 `Proc` row (`Command`,
  `Child::wait`, `Signals::recv`), ROOT-4 (no public fields, cannot be made from data).
- `design/reference.md` 6.1: `Proc` row says only "`command(prog) -> Command` (Rust's builder)",
  the same words 6.3 uses for the inert `OpenOptions`; 6.1's `&self` bullet; 12.3 paths table.
- Rust std: `Child { pub stdin: Option<ChildStdin>, pub stdout: .., pub stderr: .. }`;
  `Stdio: From<File>`.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N1, N2; `reviews/round33-consistency.md` N3.

## Scope

In scope: in 03, decide how `Child`'s pipes are reached under ROOT-4 (keep Rust's public fields
and narrow ROOT-4, or methods), classify `ChildStdin`/`ChildStdout`/`ChildStderr` and `Stdio`,
and say which receivers handles take; then state in the reference pair that `Command` carries
`Proc`'s authority (unlike `OpenOptions`) and where `Child`, `Signals`, and `ReadDir` live.

Out of scope: process semantics under simulation beyond naming.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each point with reasoning; the reference or companion states it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`; detail goes to the
  companion).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction among 02, 03, and the reference pair.

## Notes

Prefer Rust's API (D18). The core reference is at 24,997 of 25,000 tokens. Docs-only: review
rounds, not converge.
close_reason: Decided in 03 §1.1/ROOT-4, stated in 02 and the reference pair; core 24,993 tokens; rounds 68-72 clean (Codex approve, round 72)

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decisions (recorded in 03 §1.1 and ROOT-4; reference pair updated):
- Child keeps Rust's public pipe fields (stdin/stdout/stderr: Option of a pipe end), so child.stdout.take() ports unchanged (D18). ROOT-4 narrowed from 'no public fields' (already false of Root) to: each capability/handle type has a private field (no struct literal or Shape construction), and a public field holds a capability or handle, an Option of one, sink config (Root::log), or test-only sim controls. Rejected: accessor methods (break the universal Rust idiom; ROOT-4's purpose is construction, not field visibility).
- ChildStdin/ChildStdout/ChildStderr are resource handles with Proc's authority (kind proc); reads/writes suspend.
- Stdio: piped/inherit/null take no capability; From only for File and the three pipe ends; From<io::Stdout>/<io::Stderr> dropped (sink handles, not fds), and From<OwnedFd>/PipeReader/PipeWriter dropped. Stdio can hold a handle, so not Pure.
- Command is a resource handle carrying Proc's authority, unlike Pure OpenOptions; ambient Command::new stays FX0501.
- Receivers: capability types take &self; handles keep Rust's receivers, except Child::wait_with_output takes &mut self (round 70 B1: a consuming checkpoint must return its value inside the cancellation error per TASK-3, which io::Error cannot hold). Tide-only methods: File::sync, read_owned, write_owned, Signals::recv take &self; File::close takes self.
- Paths: std::process for Command, Child, pipe ends, Stdio, Signal, Signals; std::fs for ReadDir, DirEntry (companion 20; core 12.3 unchanged for budget, Rust's paths).
Core count 24,993. Reviews: rounds 68, 69, 71 (Opus), 70 (Codex).

title: Define the Ferox parent-directory manifest and workspace discovery ergonomics beyond the root-local bootstrap path
description: The bootstrap package-loading contract now explicitly allows root-local discovery, but the specs already acknowledge parent-directory discovery as a likely later ergonomics refinement. This task should define whether and how Ferox searches upward for package/workspace roots, how it resolves ambiguity, and how that behavior fits the machine-readable package-loading contract without reintroducing Cargo-style hidden complexity.
design: Primary question: what deterministic parent-directory discovery rule, if any, should Ferox adopt after the root-local bootstrap phase? Define: 1. when commands search upward for a manifest root; 2. how package roots and workspace roots are distinguished; 3. how ambiguity and nested-workspace cases are handled; 4. what machine-readable discovery facts and diagnostics are emitted; 5. what remains intentionally out of scope compared with Cargo.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: whether parent-directory discovery exists; how root selection works; what diagnostics and machine-readable facts are exposed; and what UX tradeoffs Ferox accepts. Include worked examples for subdirectory invocation, rejected ambiguous alternatives, validation expectations for discovery success/failure cases, and logging expectations for root-selection traces.

title: Decide origin syntax: from clauses vs Rust lifetime syntax by a held-out trial
description:
Decide how Ferox spells origins (borrow sources) by a held-out learnability trial.

Context: design/01-design.md D2 replaces Rust's named lifetimes with origins. The semantics are fixed in design/02-memory.md; only the spelling is open. The current spelling uses `from` clauses (`fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&str from self.src>`, struct reference fields without `<'a>`), and accepts named lifetimes that map exactly onto origins as a legacy spelling the formatter rewrites. reviews/round2-simplicity.md argues that because the meanings match, D1's rule (keep Rust's spelling wherever the meaning is the same) favors Rust lifetime syntax. D0 keeps D1/D2 syntax provisional until E1 decides it.

Method:
- Write a held-out task set of about ten tasks that design/reference.md does not mirror, heavy on borrowing: parsers and lexers over &str, iterators over borrowed data, structs holding references from one or several sources, functions returning borrows from several inputs, closures capturing borrows.
- Make two reference variants that differ only in origin spelling: (A) `from` clauses as today; (B) Rust lifetime syntax under Ferox's rules (per-field origins and elision still apply).
- Run a fresh agent per arm that reads only its variant, then grade both arms with one independent grader using the rubric in trials/e1/grading.md.

Acceptance:
- trials/e1-origins/ holds both arms' programs, notes, and a grading with first-check pass rate, borrow-related error counts, and iterations to green per arm.
- design/01-design.md D2 records the chosen spelling with that evidence, and design/reference.md and design/02-memory.md use it.

Cheapest falsifier: if arm B's borrow-related error rate is no worse than arm A's, Rust spelling wins under D1.
close_reason: done

title: Apply D18's dialect changes to the decision record, chapters, and reference
description:
Owner decision (2026-10-19, fx-7qu): D18's feasibility spike passed, with checker architecture A then B (design/01-design.md D18). This bead applies D18's listed changes to the other decisions, the chapters, and the reference, so the design describes the dialect instead of the new language.

Sources: design/01-design.md D18 ("Changes to apply to the other decisions"); research/15-rust-dialect.md (classification tables, F2, Spike results); spikes/d18/ (working spellings: facade/src, macros/src, examples/).

Changes (from D18):
- D1: contracts as #[requires]/#[ensures]; loop invariants as invariant!(..) under a fn-level #[invariants] (or any contract attribute); main as #[tide::main] fn main(root: Root) (spike-preferred; add the checker rule that tests cannot call main); modules declared with mod; .rs files.
- D2: drop the T: Owned formatter rewrite; keep 'static.
- D3: float observers and math via Tide functions (float::bits, math::sin, float::min/max); inherent methods banned by the allowlist.
- D5: stack overflow aborts (as Rust); under the simulator it fails the seed.
- D7: admission allowlist (core/alloc/std inherent methods, raw pointers inadmissible); #[trusted_pure] instead of unsafe impl Pure; companion supertraits instead of dyn Trait + Pure; Pure checked at obligations and dyn coercions.
- D10: attribute contract spelling; contract modes from the manifest and item attributes.
- D12: backends (pinned nightly rustc + LLVM; interpreter optional), checker architecture A then B, origin cross-check becomes the build; edit-loop target served by B.
- D13: direct Rust crate import with RUST-2 wrappers; facade injection via `std = { package = "tide_std" }` for Rust consumers.
- D14: typed hole spelling (todo!() stays; _?name becomes a toolchain form).
- The Tiers table (v0 core: agent toolchain on rustc builds, not the interpreter then Cranelift), the Feel example, chapters 02-04, and design/reference.md (keep it under its 25,000-token budget).

Method: edit 01 first (it owns decisions), then chapters and reference; run a review round (docs-only design work uses review rounds, not converge) and record it in reviews/.

Acceptance: 01, chapters 02-04, and reference.md describe the dialect consistently, with no remaining new-language-only spellings or backends outside history; a review round finds no v0-blocking contradiction; D18's "changes to apply" list is marked applied. Cheapest falsifier: grep for bare `requires`/`ensures` clauses, `fn main(root: Root)` without #[tide::main], `unsafe impl Pure`, `dyn .* + Pure`, `T: Owned`, and C/Cranelift backend text in design/.

title: Define the exact Ferox contract/spec syntax and erasure boundary for the first optional verification layer
description: The staged verification direction is now clear, but the exact first-layer syntax and erasure rules are still open. This task should define the concrete Ferox surface for requires/ensures/invariants/spec functions/ghost code, how those forms remain narrow and optional, and how erasure boundaries and diagnostics work without turning the language proof-first.
design: Primary question: what exact syntax and semantic boundary should Ferox adopt for its first optional verification layer? Define: 1. contract attachment syntax for functions and possibly data invariants; 2. pure spec-function and ghost-code forms; 3. erasure/runtime boundaries; 4. interaction with ownership, borrowing, and machine-readable tooling outputs; 5. explicit non-goals reserved for deeper proof layers.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what the first contract/spec syntax looks like; what ghost/spec code may do; what gets erased; how diagnostics and machine-readable outputs report verification issues; and what deeper proof constructs remain deferred. Include at least two concrete examples, rejected alternatives, validation expectations for verified/rejected/erasure cases, and tracing expectations for verification obligations and ghost stripping.

title: Respell v1 proof forms and field-borrow declarations as valid Rust under D18
description:
## Why

D18 makes every Tide program a valid Rust 2024 crate, but the v1 proof forms
and field-borrow declarations are still written in draft 3.5's grammar,
which rustc cannot parse. 01 D10's last bullet and D2 record this as
pending: the spelling is decided before v1, and E1 does not cover it.
Until it is decided, 04 describes a v1 that cannot exist under D18.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md` D10, last bullet: v1's proof forms (`spec fn`,
  `proof fn`, `law fn`, `ghost let`, proof blocks, views, spec integer
  types) must become attributes, toolchain `!` forms, or library types.
- `design/01-design.md` D2: field borrows (`fn advance(&mut self.{pos})`)
  are not Rust; their spelling (a source transform or Rust's view types) is
  open until v1.
- `design/04-contracts.md` §0 "Spelling" and §1.2 grammar: the v1 forms are
  labeled as draft 3.5 grammar pending respelling; `tide` fences mark the
  blocks that use them.
- `design/02-memory.md` §7: field-borrow syntax labeled as not Rust.
- `research/15-rust-dialect.md`, v1 table: `prove`, `spec fn`, `decreases`,
  laws are "Lib: attributes, as Prusti, Creusot, and Verus show";
  field-borrow declarations are "Open".
- Already decided in fx-pcb (keep): `#[requires]`, `#[ensures]`,
  `#[decreases]`, `#[diverges]`, `decreases!`, `#[invariant(..)]` on types,
  `requires!`/`ensures!` in closures, `hole!(goal)`. The `!` clause forms
  are rewritten by the enclosing function attribute and not exported,
  because an attribute and a `!` macro cannot share a name (E0252).

## Scope

In scope:
- A spelling for each v1 form: `spec fn`, `proof fn`, `closed spec fn`,
  `law fn` (trait items and impl discharges), `ghost let`, `proof { }`
  blocks, `assert ... by(..)`, `assume`, `reveal`, `x@` views, `int`/`nat`
  and `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` spec types, `#![trigger]`/`#[trigger]`,
  `choose`, and field-borrow declarations.
- Decision text in `design/01-design.md` (D2, D10) first, then
  `design/04-contracts.md` (§0, §1.1–§1.7, grammar, examples),
  `design/02-memory.md` §7, and Appendix A of `design/reference-companion.md`.
- A review round recorded in `reviews/`.

Out of scope:
- v0 spellings and semantics (fixed by fx-pcb and rounds 12–15).
- Implementing macros or the checker; a throwaway spike under `spikes/` is
  allowed only to show a candidate parses and lowers.

## Acceptance

- Every v1 proof form and field-borrow declaration has a valid Rust 2024
  spelling recorded in 01, with the prior art it follows (Creusot,
  Prusti, Verus) and the rejected alternatives.
- 04's examples parse as Rust (no `tide` fences left for these forms), and
  the "pending respelling" labels are gone.
- A review round finds no contradiction among 01, 02, 04, and the
  reference.

## Implementation Notes

1. Survey how Creusot (`#[logic]`, `#[predicate]`, `proof_assert!`,
   `snapshot!`, `ghost!`), Prusti (`#[pure]`, `prusti_assert!`), and
   Verus (`verus!{}`) spell each form; prefer the Prusti/Creusot style
   D18 already uses for clauses.
2. Decide per form in 01; keep `#[spec]` (executable spec functions)
   distinct from ghost spec functions.
3. Check each spelling compiles as an attribute or `!` form on the pinned
   rustc (a scratch crate is enough).
4. Update 04, 02 §7, and the companion's Appendix A; run a review round.

## Verification

- `grep -nE "spec fn|proof fn|law fn|ghost let|proof \{|\.\{" design/*.md`
  returns only history or rejected-spelling mentions.
- `grep -n '```tide' design/04-contracts.md` returns nothing.
- The review file in `reviews/` has verdict approve.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask the owner if a form has no valid Rust spelling without an
  unstable feature (D18 passes `-Zallow-features=`).
- Stop if respelling would change a v1 meaning rather than its spelling.

## Maintenance Notes

- D18's reversal conditions include E1 rejecting attribute spellings; this
  bead adds more attribute spellings, so a later E1 round on `prove` should
  cover them.
- Docs-only design work: review rounds, not converge (GOVERNANCE.md).

title: E1 gate machinery: writer broker, session coordinator, and isolation canaries
description:
## Why

fx-o8o's harness (trials/e1-checked/harness.py) renders tasks, prepares sessions, runs ./check and
./test with budgets and snapshots, and grades, but states it 'is not a gate-session coordinator'.
trials/e1-checked/readiness.md leaves to fx-ic2: the broker that dispatches a writer's logical
./check and ./test to `harness.py command SESSION MODE`, isolation canaries, toolchain and model
identities, and confirmation that the Nix store holds no repository copy. None of it depends on the
std prerequisites, so it is split out of fx-ic2 (plan review, 2026-11-09) to run now.

## Scope

In trials/e1-checked/ only. Protocol, tasks and thresholds do not change, except the two owner-decided
protocol text edits in Acceptance; a problem found in the frozen protocol goes on fx-ic2 as a comment.
- Writer harness and broker (protocol §3, §4): one fresh writer session per (task, arm, replicate)
  with the one recorded model and agent harness, whose only tools are reading and writing files in
  its directory and the logical ./check and ./test, dispatched by the broker to harness.py; no other
  shell, network, web search, repository or other-session access.
- Coordinator: the 120 triples in the order `random.Random(20261031).shuffle` fixes (§3), bounded
  batches with raw logs on disk, one rerun after an infrastructure fault (counted), first- and
  final-snapshot grading through `harness.py grade`.
- Isolation canaries for both arms (§10.3): from inside the sandbox, reading a repository file,
  another session's directory, a suite or a reference solution, a network connection beyond
  loopback, and an inherited environment variable each fail; the Nix store holds no repository copy.
- The Rust arm's test fixtures on a tmpfs TMPDIR (fx-ic2 comment, 2026-11-08 06:24).
- An identity record template (§3, §5): toolchains, crates/ revision, Cargo.lock hash, model and
  harness versions, harness revision.
Do not freeze the suites or start gate writers: both are fx-ic2's. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply.

## Acceptance

python3 trials/e1-checked/harness_test.py covers the coordinator's order and rerun rule and passes;
a canary run reports every forbidden access failing in both arms; a dry run with a scripted
stand-in writer on two tasks per arm goes through the broker only, is refused on its 21st run and
at the 40-minute limit, and produces first and final grades. No real gate writer runs.

Also (owner decision 2026-11-09, recorded on fx-ic2): edit trials/e1-checked/protocol.md §10.2 item 3 so that FX0920, FX0921 and FX0516 are excluded from E1 gating, citing that decision. This is a protocol text change, so it goes through the docs review round.

Then §10.1's sentence 'Every bead in the table blocks fx-ic2' and §10.2(1) match the dependency graph. readiness.md stays as written: it is a dated record at 31a9800, true at epic level, and the next readiness run cites the child owners.

title: Unix-domain socket capability with peer credentials
description:
## Why
Tide has no Unix-domain socket capability (research/15-rust-dialect.md:386-388). Eon's Runtime, Orbit and CLI talk over Unix sockets and authorize peers with SO_PEERCRED (Eon docs/CONTRACTS.md, EON-C31/C38).

## Scope
Bind, connect and accept on Unix-domain sockets through a capability, with the peer's uid/gid/pid as data on a capability-bounded handle, and simulated loopback like fx-hxw's TCP. Design first: where the capability lives (Net or its own), attenuation, and the simulation model.

## Acceptance
- Two tasks in one simulation exchange bytes over a simulated Unix socket deterministically per seed.
- Real loopback works in the harness sandbox.
- Peer credentials are returned on both backends.
- Toolchain tests execute each item.

Source: eon-desk proposal (/home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/eon-desk/tide-beads-from-eon.md) from an Opus assessment (tide-in-eon-report.md): use Eon as a reference workload; do not adopt Tide in Eon yet. Filed on Lucca's relayed approval (2026-11-12, via eon-desk): "if applicable, you can open beads in tide, so it can eventually serve eon better". Must not displace E1 or the first demo (fx-ic2, fx-nkv); Eon takes priority over Tide.

title: Decide whether a spawn under Tasks::limit suspends and how it meets cancellation
description:
## Why

Under `Tasks::limit(n)`, `spawn` waits for a free slot (`design/reference.md` 7.1), but 03 §1.2
lists `Scope`'s waits as "none", and the Tasks row in §1.1 does not list `spawn` among the
operations that suspend. So the chapter never says whether a limited `spawn` suspends, whether it is
a checkpoint, or what it returns when its scope is cancelled while it waits. Found by round 73 while
reviewing fx-nyy; predates it.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 Tasks row, §1.2 `Scope` row, §6.1, TASK-3.
- `design/reference.md` 7.1 (`limit` and `spawn`).
- `reviews/round73-consistency.md` (out-of-scope findings).

## Scope

In scope: decide whether a `spawn` under `limit` suspends, whether it is a checkpoint, and its
behavior in a cancelled scope (`spawn` takes `self` and returns `Task`, so it has no error to
carry cancellation); align §1.1, §1.2, and the reference.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides it with reasoning; §1.1, §1.2, and the reference agree.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.
close_reason: Decided in 03 §6.1/TASK-3, core 7.1, companion 15.2: a limited spawn is a checkpoint; in a cancelled calling scope it starts nothing. Reviews: rounds 80-83, 85 (Opus), 84, 86 (Codex, approve). Follow-ups: fx-0ai.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decision (03 §0 Checkpoint, §1.1 Tasks row, §1.2 Scope row, §6.1 new paragraph, TASK-5; core 7.1 Bounded concurrency):
Under Tasks::limit(n), Scope::spawn waits for a free slot. The wait suspends but is shielded like a join: not a checkpoint, never interrupted by cancellation. In a cancelled scope spawn still waits, the child still starts and observes cancellation at its first checkpoint, so TASK-2/TASK-4 decide outcomes exactly as for an unlimited scope. The core's provisional rule becomes firm.
Reasons: spawn returns Task, not Result, so it has no error to carry a cancellation; every spawned child runs, so a child that turns cancellation into a value (companion 15.2 fetch_one) still reports one.
Rejected: (a) skipping the child in a cancelled scope (pre-cancelled Task): its join fails with no child error behind it and per-item outcomes are lost; (b) starting it immediately over the limit: breaks the attenuation; (c) making spawn a checkpoint returning Result: changes the std::thread::scope shape at every call site for a wait only limited scopes have.
Cost: a body in a cancelled limited scope drains its remaining spawns at width n; it can stop early by checking tasks.checkpoint() in its loop. The wait is as soft as deadlines (TASK-5).
Core at 24,993 of 25,000 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Addendum after round 80 (B1): the limit is one count shared by all scopes from that Tasks (matches the Semaphore mapping, companion 14.3). A task that holds a slot and waits for one (spawning into its own scope, or a nested scope from the same Tasks) can deadlock the pool, as with any semaphore; cancellation and deadlines do not break it, and the simulator reports it (§9.3). Skipping children in a cancelled scope (rejected option a) would break that deadlock only when something cancels the scope, so it stays rejected; 03 §6.1 says so and advises nested work use its own Tasks or no limit. Rejected: slot lending (a slot holder releases its slot while it waits) — more state and a new notion of 'live' for a pattern a separate Tasks avoids. N1/N3/N4/N5 fixed in text; N2 not applied (core at 24,993 of 25,000; 7.1 already states it).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Reversal after round 81 (B1). Final decision: the slot wait of a limited spawn IS a checkpoint. In a cancelled scope a limited spawn returns at once and starts nothing, even with a free slot (level-triggered, so the outcome does not depend on slot timing). The child counts as one whose first checkpoint returned the cancellation and which returned E::from(TaskError::Cancelled): TASK-2/TASK-4 apply unchanged (echo when body Err/sibling failure caused it; DeadlineExceeded when the scope's own deadline did; join returns Err(Cancelled)). TASK-3 notes it.
Reason: the count is shared across scopes from one Tasks, so slots can be held by other scopes' children that this scope's cancellation never reaches; an uninterruptible wait could outlast the scope's deadline without bound and go unreported (round 81). A checkpoint also lets a deadline or cancel() break hold-and-wait deadlocks (child spawning into its own scope or a nested scope from the same Tasks); otherwise the simulator reports a global deadlock.
Cost: an unstarted child cannot turn cancellation into a value. Companion 15.2 therefore drops its scope deadline and relies on the operation deadline it already passes to net.get (a late-starting child gets Timeout at once). 03's 12.2 example uses an unlimited scope and is unaffected.
Superseded: the earlier shielded-wait decision and its addendum. Still rejected: starting over the limit (breaks attenuation); spawn returning Result (a ? on every spawn).
Core 7.1 states it plus a one-line deadlock warning (round 81 N3); core at 24,995 of 25,000.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Refinement after round 82 (B1, N1-N4): the limited spawn observes the CALLING task's cancellation (TASK-3). It drops f unrun and, like any checkpoint returning a cancellation, sets the caller's echo bit; the child's join returns Err(Cancelled). If the scope spawned into is itself cancelled, the 'as if cancelled at its first checkpoint and propagated' rule applies (TASK-2/TASK-4 unchanged). If not (a task in a cancelled nested scope spawning into an enclosing scope passed down), the unstarted child is an echo and that scope is unaffected, so one request's deadline cannot cancel a server scope. Not applied: 14.3 timeout row and 03 §6.5 deadlock pointer (nits).

title: State the Pure status of simulator objects (sim.world, faults, nodes, LogConfig)
description:
## Why

The `Pure` status of the simulator's own objects is never stated: `sim.world`, `sim.faults`,
`SimNode`, `NodeTask`, and `Root`'s `log: LogConfig` field. A test helper that takes one of these
cannot tell whether a `Pure` bound or a `par_map` capture accepts it. The risk is low because
they exist only in test code, but 02 §9 claims to own the full table. Found by round 32 (N4).

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §9.2 (`sim.world`, `sim.faults`, `sim.node`), §9.5
  (nodes, `NodeRoot`); `design/reference.md` 6.2 (`Root`'s `log` field), 6.8; companion 17
  (`SimNode`, `NodeTask`, provisional).
- `design/02-memory.md` §9: none of these appear.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N4.

## Scope

In scope: classify each object (most act on the simulated world without a capability argument,
so they are resource handles of the simulated capabilities and not `Pure`; `LogConfig` may be
plain configuration), and state it in 02 §9 or 03 §9.2, with a companion line if agents need it.

Out of scope: changing simulator APIs.

## Acceptance

- Each named object's `Pure` status is stated once, in its owner, and the other documents agree.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds. Avoid core reference changes (24,997 of 25,000 tokens).
close_reason: 02 §9 states the Pure status of SimRoot, NodeRoot, sim.world's type, Faults, SimNode, NodeTask, and LogConfig; companion §17 points to it. Reviews fx-t99-r1 (Opus, Codex), r2 (Opus), r3 (Codex) approve.

title: Decide OnceLock and Sync-mutation types in the Pure table (owner decision)
description:
## Why

02 §9 owns the `Pure` table, but reference 6.6 and 03 §3.1 call more types not-`Pure` than 02
does, and nothing says whether a local (non-static) `OnceLock` is admitted at all. If one were
admitted and `Pure`, a `par_map` closure calling `get_or_init` on a shared `&OnceLock` would
observe which branch ran first, breaking 02's determinism guarantee for parallel regions. Found
by round 32 (N3) and round 33 (N4) while reviewing fx-zm4.

## Evidence

- `design/reference.md` 6.6: synchronization handles include "`OnceLock`, and any `Sync` type
  whose `&self` API can observe or cause mutation".
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §3.1: not-`Pure` includes "everything in
  `std::sync::raw`"; §1.2: `Mutex`, `RwLock`, and weak atomics live in `std::sync::raw`.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9 "`Pure`: no authority reachable": lists neither `OnceLock`, the
  general `Sync`-mutation rule, nor `std::sync::raw`.
- 03 GLOBAL table and companion 14.1 forbid `static` `OnceLock`/`LazyLock` (`FX0502`), but say
  nothing about a local one.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N3, `reviews/round33-consistency.md` N4.

## Decision needed (owner)

Is a local `OnceLock` (and `LazyLock`, `OnceCell`) admitted? Options: (a) admitted, created
with `&Tasks` like other synchronization handles, and not `Pure`; (b) rejected by ADMIT-1
(`FX0520`), with a pattern to use instead; (c) admitted and `Pure` only when `!Sync`
(`OnceCell`). Recommend before writing; this changes which programs check.

## Scope

In scope: the decision above; make 02 §9 the single statement of the not-`Pure` set (add
`std::sync::raw`, the `OnceLock` outcome, and decide whether to keep reference 6.6's general
"any `Sync` type whose `&self` API can observe or cause mutation" rule, and if so state it in
02); align 03 §1.2/§3.1 and reference 6.6.

Out of scope: other `Pure` questions (resource handles were settled by fx-zm4).

## Acceptance

- 02 §9, 03 §3.1, and reference 6.6 name the same not-`Pure` set.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds. The core reference is at 24,997 of 25,000 tokens (companion "Core
count" line); any core change must be paid for by a cut. Stop and ask before changing 01 D7 or
D9.
close_reason: OnceLock/LazyLock rejected (FX0520); OnceCell/LazyCell Pure; 02 §9, 03 §3.1/§3.3/ADMIT-1, reference 6.4/6.6/6.9, companion 14.1 aligned; rounds 34-35 (approve with notes, resolutions applied); core 24,969 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision (2026-10-20): (b) OnceLock and LazyLock are rejected by ADMIT-1 (FX0520); fix: build the value before spawning, or Shared<Option<T>> with `with`. OnceCell and LazyCell stay admitted and Pure (not Sync, task-local like Cell). Reference 6.6's general 'any Sync type whose &self API can observe or cause mutation' rule is replaced by a structural rule in 02 §9: a type with a user-written `unsafe impl Sync` is a synchronization handle, so not Pure unless #[trusted_pure]. Fits D7's existing 'synchronization handle' term; no D7/D9 change. Reason: OnceLock/LazyLock shared by & in par_map make the winning branch observable (init value, sink output, panic); their remaining Tide use (cross-task lazy init) is covered by Shared::with; the general rule was not structurally decidable.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision revised (2026-10-20), after round 34 B2: drop the 'user-written unsafe impl Sync => not Pure' clause. Reason: it conflicts with D7's Pure definition unless D7 is edited, changes no verdict for sound code (a sound Sync type mutating through &self synchronizes via atomics, locks, raw pointers, or FFI, all already not Pure), and falsely flags &mut-only UnsafeCell wrappers. 03 §3.3 instead states the structural argument: std's Sync interior-mutable types are listed or rejected; outside std, Sync needs unsafe impl Sync, a trust hole under the unsafe grant whose soundness obligation covers this, as for unsafe impl Send. No D7 change. The OnceLock/LazyLock decision (b) stands.

title: Enforce every FX rule the reference names in tide-admit
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) compares Tide writers against Rust writers. If the driver does not reject
code that breaks a rule the reference teaches (for example a lossy `as`, FX0301), a Tide writer can
pass with code that is not Tide, and the comparison flatters Tide. No bead owns enforcing the FX
rules beyond fx-kw8's allowlist, `Pure`, and authority checks: `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md`
§10.1 lists this as E1-P14.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P14, §10.2 item 3)`
- `design/reference.md (every FX code it names)`
- `conformance/README.md (AWAITS CHECKER cases)`
- `reviews/fx-gfq-r1-codex.md (finding 2)`

## Scope

Make tide-admit report, with the stated code and at the reference's severity, every violation
of a rule whose FX code design/reference.md names: reject the error-level ones, including FX0301 (lossy `as`), the macro and derive codes, globals,
`Root` misuse, async, thread::spawn, Mutex/select habits, catch_unwind, ignored `Result` (FX0702),
unused imports (FX0913), and the contract-placement codes, and report the lint-level ones
(FX0508, FX0607, FX0608) as lints without rejecting the crate. Conformance case marks record
only errors today, so the runner needs a lint mark for these cases. Split into child slices if one session
cannot finish it. No new language semantics.

## Acceptance

For every FX code that design/reference.md names, a conformance case violating it gets that code
from the driver at the reference's severity (rejected for an error, reported without rejection for
a lint), and `conformance/run.sh` reports no AWAITS CHECKER line for those codes.
acceptance_criteria: For every FX code that design/reference.md names, a conformance case violating it gets that code from the driver at the reference's severity (rejected for an error, reported without rejection for a lint), and conformance/run.sh reports no AWAITS CHECKER line for those codes. title: tide-admit keeps FX diagnostics when a trait path fails to resolve
description:
## Why

An unresolved trait in a bound or trait-ref position (for example `fn b<F: Missing>(_: F)`, `impl std::future::Future for S`, or `use std::future::Future;` with Tide's std) suppresses every HIR-walk diagnostic in the file. The file then shows only rustc's E0432/E0433 and no FX code, including unrelated ones on other lines. An unresolved *type* (`fn b(_: Missing)`) keeps them. The AST check (`async fn`, FX0601) survives, so the loss is in the HIR walk that `check_crate` runs (crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs:84). rustc still rejects every such file, so nothing wrong is admitted. But a writer whose file has one unresolved trait loses all of Tide's rule feedback, which E1's iteration measures depend on.
