comments.text: From fx-nkv.4 review (2026-11-10, Opus finding 2): Shared::with reserves a FIFO ticket before blocking. Multi-cell ops must reserve tickets lazily, on each cell only after acquiring the previous one in id order; reserving on all operands up front can deadlock (X: A#0, Y: A#1, Y: B#0, X: B#1).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-11 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-proc/report.md; the report lands in research/ as 26-process-io-and-shared-sets.md with whichever of fx-5vj/fx-ugm lands first, and the other cites it): adopt the report's §B recommendations.
1. Acquisition: sort operands by cell id; ascending, reserve each ticket lazily, wait until served, keep its guard; run f; advance serving on every cell, drop guards, notify_all each. 'Atomically' = f runs only with all held, no partial acquisition visible, no scheduling point inside the set. Make with the one-cell case of a private acquire_set/release_set pair (one owner of the ticket protocol; keep with's single unconditional advance/drop/notify step that fx-nkv.4's rebuttal relies on).
2. Ids: real cells from one static AtomicU64 (fetch_add, Relaxed); simulated cells use fx-nkv.5's id; one private order_key(). Before sorting, check every operand's domain: mixed real/simulated or two simulations panic (fx-nkv.5 decision 2).
3. Aliases: detected in the sort pass before the first ticket; Aliased wins over Poisoned (LOCK-2); no ticket taken.
4. Poison: stop at the first poisoned cell (consume that ticket, release all held, Err(Poisoned), f doesn't run, no cell changes); a panic in f poisons every held cell before release (LOCK-6), then release, notify, resume_unwind. f gets &mut [&mut T] in the caller's order (sort guards back by original index; safe Rust). reset(&self, v) clears poison, drops the old payload after release, allowed on a healthy cell.
5. Simulator: one point before the first reservation, none between cells, one after the last release; one cell acquire event per operand ascending and release events descending, all at that step; wait state 'ready at cells(ids ascending)'. with_all(&[]) takes the points as any call. FIFO is per cell by arrival.
6. Equivalence: delete the stub's unimplemented! with2/same/with_all block in the same change; move conformance/rules.md LOCK-2/3/6 rows from deferred to covered.

title: Port conformance/run.sh to a Rust test target
description:
## Why

`conformance/run.sh` (149 lines of bash and awk) has become the corpus's verdict engine: it parses
`//~` marks with awk, scrapes rustc's and the driver's short-format diagnostics with awk, and
decides binary versus library with `grep '^fn main'`, a heuristic that forced a dummy `fn main`
into `root_no_main.rs` (fx-kw8.8) and bit fx-nkv.1's `root_main_nested.rs`.

Decision (2026-11-01, agent, after a web research pass at the owner's request to pick among Rust,
xtask, mise tasks, Python, and Nushell): port it to Rust as a `harness = false` integration test
target in the root workspace. Reasons: compiler UI-test runners in the Rust ecosystem are Rust
(rustc's compiletest; `ui_test`, used through `harness = false`), and the corpus already follows
their `//~`/`//@` conventions; a test target runs under `cargo test` with no new tool; the stable
oracle can use `--error-format=json` instead of text scraping; mark parsing gets types and unit
tests. Rejected: xtask (a workspace-automation convention, not a test mechanism); `ui_test` as a
dependency (its `//~ LEVEL: msg` grammar differs from Tide's per-line code lists, two compilers,
two modes, and the AWAITS CHECKER verdict; adopting it means rewriting every case's marks; revisit
if the formats converge); mise tasks (adds a tool and still leaves the logic in shell); Python (a
second runtime and no types for the verdict logic); Nushell (still working toward 1.0 stability,
and niche for agent authors). `scripts/autorun.sh`, `scripts/handoff-guard.sh`, and the
spike and trial scripts stay shell.

## Scope

Replace `conformance/run.sh` with a Rust test target (for example `cargo test --test conformance`)
that keeps the case format, verdicts (PASS, AWAITS CHECKER, FAIL), the `--trace` listing, and the
stable-rustc oracle plus pinned-driver checks. Decide crate type from the case explicitly (a `//@`
directive or rustc's own entry detection), not by grep. Update README.md, conformance/README.md,
AGENTS.md's Verification section (through `.agent-protocols.local.md`, then re-render), and every
open bead whose Acceptance names `conformance/run.sh`.

## Acceptance

The Rust runner gives the same verdict per case as `conformance/run.sh` on the full corpus
(compare both outputs once before deleting the script), runs with stdin closed and exits non-zero
on any FAIL, and `cargo test --workspace` passes.

title: Decide strict, tagged codecs without serde

## Scope
Design decision only: how Tide's codec (std::codec / std::json) expresses strict decoding and tagged enums without serde, or a recorded reason not to. Implementation, if any, gets its own bead.

## Acceptance
A recorded decision in the owning design chapter, with research cited, a tier, and follow-up beads if any.

title: Production std provides Arc, sync::Weak and dbg! as the reference promises
description:
## Why

Reference §1 lists `Arc` (created with `&Tasks`, minus count observers, §6.4) and `Weak` among the standard types that keep their Rust API (design/reference.md:35-36). §2.1 lists `dbg!` (an error in release builds, FX0507; reference.md:57), and §6.5 routes it to stderr in debug builds (reference.md:461). Production tide-std provides none of them. crates/tide-std/src/lib.rs:219-222 lists "the `dbg` and `trace` sinks" and "other `sync` items" as not provided yet, and crates/tide-std/src/sync.rs has `Shared` and channels but no public `Arc` or `Weak`. Only the conformance stub std (conformance/rustc/std/src/lib.rs) declares them, with unimplemented bodies.

A Tide-arm E1 writer who follows the reference to `use std::sync::Arc`, or who reaches for `dbg!`, gets E0432 or "cannot find macro" against production std. That reads as a language failure. fx-yg5.5's acceptance does not catch it: its check covers solutions that compile, and the harness looks for FX0520. Found by the fx-yg5.5 reviews (Codex r1 finding 1; Opus r2 finding 2, /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-fx-yg5.5-work/).

## Scope

Provide them in production tide-std, matching the reference and the conformance stub's signatures:
- `std::sync::Arc`, with creation through `&Tasks` and without `strong_count`, `weak_count`, `get_mut`, `try_unwrap` or `into_inner` (GLOBAL-6). `make_mut`, `downgrade` (with `&Tasks`) and the usual `Deref`/`Clone` stay.
- `std::sync::Weak`, with `upgrade`.
- `dbg!`, writing to stderr in debug builds. Release builds keep FX0507 as tide-admit enforces it, and nothing changes there.

Keep the `Pure`/`Send` treatment that §2.2 and chapter 03 give these types; check them against the conformance cases GLOBAL-6 and SINK rows already carry. Update lib.rs's "not provided yet" list. No reference change; if one proves necessary, the holder of design/reference.md makes it. Held-out rule: draw nothing from trials/e1-checked/.

## Acceptance

The existing conformance cases for GLOBAL-6 (global_arc_accept, global_arc_count, global_arc_payload) and an accepted `dbg!` case build and run against production std, not only the stub, through the production-std build test. `cargo test --workspace` and `conformance/run.sh` pass.
close_reason: Landed dd3cd13: production tide-std provides Arc, Weak and dbg!. Arc/Weak schedule in simulation (new, downgrade, make_mut, both upgrade phases), and payload access is plain. Landing proof on d7ae706: workspace 286/0, conformance 335 PASS / 5 AWAITS / 0 FAIL, harness 69 OK, all 30 E1 references pass. Follow-ups are on fx-djp.

title: Describe Tide as a capability-safe, replayable subset of Rust
description:
## Why
The fx-tcde/fx-k778 Opus review noted that the headline 'Capability-safe, replayable Rust' and the plain form 'Rust that can't overreach' use 'Rust' as Tide's own descriptor. The Rust trademark policy says the marks may not be used to refer to another programming language or a modified Rust (research/28 §3). Owner, 2026-11-13: "update it only if you find a better description".

Coordinator decision: 'A capability-safe, replayable subset of Rust' is better on accuracy as well as risk. It states D18 literally (every Tide program is a valid Rust 2024 crate), names Tide's relation to Rust rather than calling Tide Rust, and stays as short as a tagline needs.

## Scope
README headline and intro, the Thesis one-liner in design/01-design.md, and research/28 §2-3 (the comparison row and the adopted/rejected definitions). No other wording changes.

## Acceptance
No repo doc outside archive/ and reviews/ uses 'Rust' alone as Tide's descriptor (grep for 'replayable Rust' and 'Rust that can'), every changed claim matches D18, and the docs-only review (Codex pass, then an Opus round) approves.

title: Define Ferox line span semantics with and without trailing line breaks
description: Formatter and diagnostics work is cleaner if Ferox explicitly distinguishes a line span excluding the trailing line break from a span including it. This task should define those concepts, where each is used, and how they map onto the authoritative span model.
design: Primary question: should Ferox explicitly model both the logical span of a line excluding its terminator and the physical span including the trailing line break? Define where each form is used, how they compose with byte-authoritative spans, and how formatter and diagnostics code should request the right one.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task defines both line-span concepts, names their intended uses, clarifies newline-edge cases such as final lines without terminators and CRLF, and explains how diagnostics and formatting avoid ambiguity by using the right span flavor.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should explicitly model both line spans excluding the trailing line break and line spans including it. The excluding-break span should be the default logical line-content view for diagnostics text snippets, parser-facing line reasoning, and most user-facing source displays. The including-break span should be an explicit secondary view for formatter/layout logic, faithful source slicing, and operations that must preserve or reason about physical line terminators. CRLF counts as a single logical line break whose full byte extent belongs only to the including-break span. Final lines without terminators have identical excluding/including spans. Rationale: Roslyn's TextLine model shows this split removes ambiguity around line boundaries and keeps formatting and diagnostics from overloading one span concept. Apply in v1 immediately as part of the bootstrap source contract, before formatter and richer diagnostics behavior harden further. This is a small foundational distinction, not a later optimization feature.

title: Settle D18 review notes before the checker's test corpus
description:
## Why

Review rounds 12–15 on the D18 application (fx-pcb) approved v0 with no
blocking contradiction, but left notes the reviewers said must be settled
before the checker's conformance test corpus is written. Each is an
under-specified rule or a small inconsistency a test would have to guess.

## Evidence

Each note's full text, with file:line evidence and a proposed fix, is in
the review file named:

- `reviews/round12-consistency.md`:
  - N4: float functions do not cover `from_bits`, `f32`, `mul_add`, `sqrt`.
  - N6: whether a plain `fn main()` without `#[tide::main]` is allowed;
    the habit row for it cites rustc's E0580 instead of an FX code.
  - N7: property tests need Tide's std to replace Rust's `#[test]`; no
    design text states it. `#[error]`/`#[from]`/`#[source]`/`#[codec]` are
    derive helper attributes, not proc macros.
  - N8: the Bend example's `#[ensures(.., by = ..)]` puts a top-level
    comma in a clause, against 04's one-expression rule.
  - N9: "stack overflow fails the seed" has no mechanism when the
    simulator runs in one process.
  - N11 (part): the spike's `tide-admit` reports the `Pure` check as
    `FX0510`, which the design uses for the least-authority lint.
  - N12: `design/reference.md` (about 87.7k characters, estimated 22–24k
    tokens) has never been counted against its 25,000-token budget; no
    counting script exists.
- `reviews/round13-consistency.md` N3: 04 §1.2's `trait_fn`/`impl_fn`
  grammar rules lack a tier mark; the reference does not say v0 rejects
  clauses on trait methods, or with which FX code. Also: D18 and D12 give
  different reasons for building an interpreter; RUST-6 has no tier.
- `reviews/round14-consistency.md` N3: reassigning a `&mut` parameter
  (`cur = &mut n.next`) is rejected by the spike's closure lowering
  (E0521, E0597) in any function with `#[ensures]`, and "value at return"
  is ambiguous for it, which affects `tide fix`'s rewrite to `final(*x)`.
  N4: the README's "no package code runs at build time" needs a qualifier
  for v1 imported crates.
- `reviews/round15-consistency.md` N1: whether 04 item 3's limits on
  `Clone` impls apply to implicit entry snapshots of by-value parameters
  (CLAUSE-4, `design/04-contracts.md:422–429`). N2: 01 D10 says "Under
  `prove` (v1)" for the bare-`*x` error, 04 rule 4 says "From v1". N3: the
  non-`Clone` error's fix could also add `T: Clone` in generic code.

## Scope

In scope:
- `design/01-design.md` (decisions first), `design/02-memory.md`,
  `design/03-authority-concurrency.md`, `design/04-contracts.md`,
  `design/reference.md`, `README.md`.
- A token count of `design/reference.md` with a stated, repeatable method
  (a small script under `scripts/` is fine if the owner agrees; otherwise
  record the method and number in the reference header).

Out of scope:
- Respelling v1 proof forms and field-borrow declarations (separate bead).
- Renumbering codes inside `spikes/d18/` (throwaway); note the mapping
  instead.
- Any change of v0 meaning beyond what a note requires.

## Acceptance

- Every note listed above is fixed in the design text or recorded in 01's
  Open Questions with a reason it can wait past the corpus.
- `design/reference.md` has a measured token count under 25,000 with the
  method recorded.
- A review round finds no v0-blocking contradiction.

## Implementation Notes

1. Read each review's note and proposed fix; most are one to three
   sentences.
2. Decide the semantic ones in 01 first (N6 `main`, N9 simulator overflow,
   round 14 N3 `&mut` reassignment, round 15 N1 implicit clones), then
   update the chapters and reference.
3. Count reference tokens; tighten text if over budget.
4. Run a review round and record it in `reviews/`.

## Verification

- The new `reviews/` file has verdict approve.
- The token count method, rerun, reports under 25,000.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask the owner if a note needs a new language decision rather
  than a clarification (likely candidates: N6, N9, round 14 N3).
- Stop if the reference cannot fit the budget without dropping v0 content.

## Maintenance Notes

- `fx-jv9` (held-out E1 round) also measures reference token cost; reuse
  this bead's counting method there.
- Docs-only design work: review rounds, not converge (GOVERNANCE.md).
close_reason: done

title: Define a sharper ownership-aware concurrency model that makes Ferox safer to evolve without capability-lattice complexity
description: Ferox currently has a prudent but still underpowered concurrency story. This task is to define a more compelling ownership-aware concurrency direction: make ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized sharing visually and semantically distinct; identify what should remain explicit and restricted; and find a model that is safer to change than ad hoc concurrency without importing Pony/Verona-scale capability machinery.
design:
Primary question: What concurrency model makes Ferox safer to evolve while staying ownership-centered and mechanically simple?

Define the model around:
1. Concurrency modes: ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized shared mutation.
2. Surface syntax and APIs: what should be visually explicit in code.
3. Structured execution: task spawning, lifetimes, cancellation/join boundaries, and what remains out of scope.
4. Safety and change story: which race-prone or maintenance-hostile patterns are prevented by construction.

Do not import a full capability lattice. The goal is a small, explicit model that composes with Ferox ownership rules.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What are the core Ferox concurrency primitives?
- How do ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized sharing differ in syntax and semantics?
- Which concurrency patterns are intentionally disallowed to keep reasoning simple?
- Why is this model safer to change than ad hoc concurrency in comparable languages?

Include:
- a few canonical examples and one explicit list of non-goals;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for concurrency typing/checking rules, scenario tests for allowed and forbidden sharing patterns, and end-to-end scripts that exercise task spawn/join/error flows;
- detailed logging requirements for task lifecycle, ownership transfer, synchronization boundaries, and concurrency-related diagnostics.
close_reason: Defined the ownership-aware concurrency model in spec/LANGUAGE.md, V1_DIRECTION.md, and spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md, including access modes, task capture rules, non-goals, and validation expectations.

title: Record a later-performance plan for multiple text metrics without multiple authoritative position systems
description: Ferox may later need fast conversions across bytes, human-facing columns, and editor-specific encodings. This task should capture the later-performance strategy for multiple text metrics while preserving a single authoritative internal position system.
design: Primary question: how should Ferox plan for multiple text metrics later without introducing multiple authoritative position systems now? Define the later-performance stance for fast conversions across bytes, human-facing columns, and editor encodings, while keeping one canonical internal metric.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task records the canonical-metric rule, describes later conversion/indexing layers Ferox may add for performance, explains why v1 should not expose multiple authoritative coordinate systems, and notes expected validation/benchmark implications.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Name naked_asm! in the design or deny it in tide-admit
description:
## Why

The admission driver admits `naked_asm!` under the `unsafe` grant
(`crates/tide-admit/src/policy.rs:88`, `granted("core::arch::naked_asm")`), but no
design text names it: 03 ADMIT-1 and UNSAFE-1 name `asm!` and `global_asm!` only,
and reference 2.1's closed `!`-form list makes every other form `FX0103`, so the
design rejects what the driver admits. Found by fx-k0z's r1 Opus review (N6,
`reviews/fx-k0z-r1-opus.md`).

## Scope

In scope: decide whether `naked_asm!` (with `#[unsafe(naked)]`) is admitted under the
grant; record it in 03 ADMIT-1 and UNSAFE-1 and, if admitted, in reference 2.1 within
the 25,000-token budget (`scripts/count-tokens.sh`), `conformance/rules.md`'s UNSAFE-1
row, and a granted and an ungranted case; or, if not, change `policy.rs` to deny it,
with a driver test.

Out of scope: other `core::arch` items (denied with or without the grant, ADMIT-1).

## Acceptance

- Design text and `policy.rs` agree on `naked_asm!`, with a conformance case on each side.
- `conformance/run.sh` and `cargo test --workspace` exit 0.
close_reason: Landed 0692860: naked_asm! admitted only under the unsafe grant. Opus r1 clean, Codex r1 approve (reviews/fx-xrx-r1-*.md).

Evidence: `reviews/fx-k0z-r1-opus.md:159`; `research/15-rust-dialect.md:203`; `research/07-effects-capabilities.md:170`. Pinned rustc source under `lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust/compiler/`: `rustc_mir_build/src/check_unsafety.rs:516` exempts naked assembly from unsafe blocks; `rustc_hir_typeck/src/naked_functions.rs:78` checks body shape; `rustc_codegen_ssa/src/mir/naked_asm.rs:57` emits global assembly. ## Open problems / next steps

Opus chooses admission or denial, applies the chosen edits, authenticates and measures the reference against 25,000 tokens, then runs governance review and acceptance checks on that candidate. This report does not close the bead.

Skipped: implementation and landing; assembler canary/sandbox and runtime execution were not tested.

comments.text:
Opus decision (2026-11-07, claude-opus-5-5):

# fx-xrx decision (Opus, 2026-11-07)

## Decision

**Admit `naked_asm!`, with `#[unsafe(naked)]`, under the `unsafe` grant only.**
Without the grant the attribute is `FX0901` and the macro `FX0520`; under it each
is a trust hole. `policy.rs` stays as it is. The design text changes to match the
driver.

Reasons, checked against primary evidence:

- The driver already enforces this contract. `policy.rs:88` has
  `granted("core::arch::naked_asm")` ahead of the broad `core::arch::*` deny.
  `walk.rs:1120` (`unsafe_attrs`) routes `AttributeKind::Naked` through
  `granted`, and `walk.rs:1343` (`check_expansions`) routes every macro
  expansion through `use_def`. I ran the conformance runner on scratch cases
  (below): ungranted gives FX0901 on the attribute and FX0520 on the macro;
  granted passes on stable rustc and the driver. Codex's trust artifact
  (`.codex-fx-xrx/trust-artifact.json`) records two holes on the item: "an
  unsafe attribute" and "uses `core::arch::naked_asm`".
- No new trust hole. A granted package can already place arbitrary machine code
  with `global_asm!` plus an `unsafe extern` declaration, or wrap `asm!` in a
  safe `fn`. A naked function is safe to call from an ungranted package, but so
  is any safe wrapper around granted `unsafe`. RUN-5 already refuses
  `run: covered` for any branch that adds a hole or a grant, or changes a
  package with an `unsafe` grant. Assembler file reads (`.incbin`/`.include`)
  use the same global-assembly path, and RUN-2's build sandbox bounds them. A
  probe of mine: under the grant, `naked_asm!("jmp {}", sym
  core::arch::x86_64::_rdtsc)` is still `FX0520` on the driver. So a `sym`
  operand does not bypass the allowlist.
- Rust 2024's list of unsafe attributes is `no_mangle`, `export_name`,
  `link_section`, and `naked`. UNSAFE-1 lists the first three. Naming the fourth
  makes the list complete and costs nothing.

Rejected:

- **Deny `naked_asm!` in v0.** This buys no authority protection, since
  equivalent code is reachable through granted `global_asm!`. It would also
  leave `#[unsafe(naked)]` admitted under the grant but unusable, because rustc
  requires a `naked_asm!` body. And the broad `core::arch::*` deny reports
  `FX0520` where reference 2.1 promises `FX0103`, so either the reference or the
  driver would need a special case. That is more change for a smaller,
  inconsistent surface.
- **Codex's reference 2.1 draft.** It measures 25,000 tokens, which fails "under
  25,000" (reference.md:10, 00-first-principles.md:110/122). One line is not
  rewrapped (about 115 columns). It also drops "as in Rust", which tells the
  agent these macros behave as Rust's. Replaced by the text below, which
  measures 24,994.
- **Codex's 03 §2.5 rewrite.** It drops the reason the bullet exists ("places
  machine code without an `unsafe` block") and adds a sentence restating Rust's
  naked-function rules. Replaced by a minimal insertion that keeps the reason,
  which applies to `naked_asm!` too.
- **Two new case files.** Rejected in favour of extending the two existing cases
  that already own ungranted and granted assembly (`unsafe_global_asm.rs`,
  `unsafe_granted.rs`). That means fewer files, and each assembly spelling stays
  on the same side of the same case.
- **New driver test.** Not required. The policy row exists, and the shared
  `granted` path that turns it into FX0520 or a hole is already covered,
  including the hole record (`tests/driver.rs:660-720`). The conformance pair
  proves this item on both sides. Record Codex's trust-artifact observation on
  the bead as proof of the hole record.

## Implementation instructions for Codex

Work in `.worktrees/fx-xrx` (branch `fx-xrx`, base `d12d7e0`). Do not commit
`DECISION.md`, `CODEX-REPORT.md`, or `.codex-fx-xrx/`. Rewrap prose at each
file's existing width (72 to 76 columns in reference.md; keep 03's long lines
where they already are).

1. `design/01-design.md:430-431` (D7, admission allowlist). Change
   `and \`asm!\` and \`global_asm!\` without an \`unsafe\` grant.` to
   `and \`asm!\`, \`global_asm!\`, and \`naked_asm!\` without an \`unsafe\` grant.`
   Leave `01:844` alone: `#[unsafe(naked)]` is an unsafe attribute, which that
   parenthetical already includes.

2. `design/03-authority-concurrency.md`:
   - `:557-559` (§2.5 bullet). Make it exactly:
     ```
       - `global_asm!` and `naked_asm!`, which place machine code without an
         `unsafe` block, and `asm!`, in a package without an `unsafe` grant;
         under the grant they are `unsafe` holes (RUN-4);
     ```
   - `:711-712` (UNSAFE-1). Change the attribute list to
     `(\`#[unsafe(no_mangle)]\`, \`#[unsafe(export_name)]\`, \`#[unsafe(link_section)]\`, \`#[unsafe(naked)]\`)`
     and rewrap.
   - `:714`. Change `do \`asm!\` and \`global_asm!\` (\`FX0520\`, ADMIT-1)` to

title: Define the concrete Ferox source-language personality so the language feels readable, regular, and worth using
description: The high-level thesis is now much sharper than the concrete day-to-day source-language feel. This task is to define what writing normal Ferox should actually feel like: expression orientation, control-flow style, patterns, API conventions, common function shapes, and the balance between restriction and pleasantness. The goal is to turn the current FP-shaped readability direction into a more concrete source-language identity without widening the semantic core.
design:
Primary question: What should everyday Ferox code look and feel like when the language is working well?

Define the source-language personality through concrete examples:
1. Function and module shape.
2. Expression orientation versus statement-heavy style.
3. Pattern matching and destructuring norms.
4. Mutation boundaries and transformation style without relying on pipeline syntax.
5. API conventions that support readable left-to-right data flow through named steps, nested calls, or expression blocks without widening the semantic core.

This task should make Ferox feel tangible, not just principled.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What does idiomatic Ferox code look like?
- Which syntax and style choices are central to the language's identity?
- How do transformation-heavy helpers, mutation boundaries, matching, and helper functions fit together in normal code?
- What source-language moves are intentionally discouraged because they raise entropy?

Include:
- 3-5 canonical code snippets that illustrate the recommended Ferox style;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for the relevant syntax/forms, formatter and parser golden tests for the canonical snippets, and end-to-end scripts that exercise normal authoring/refactoring flows;
- detailed logging requirements for parser, formatter, and diagnostic output so source-language ergonomics issues are easy to debug.
notes: Decision: Ferox source personality should be explicit, expression-oriented, ADT-heavy, and regular. Idiomatic code uses match for typed state, named intermediates across representation or failure boundaries, small helper functions where they clarify transformations, tight local mutation, and honest public APIs built from enums, Option, and Result. Discouraged styles include flag-driven APIs, operator-driven composition, broad mutation chains, and grab-bag modules.

title: Lossless-cast replacements: truncate, cast_signed, round_from, and float TryFrom
description:
## Why

design/reference.md §4.2 makes lossy `as` FX0301 and teaches its replacements: `x.truncate()` (low
bits, target from context), `cast_unsigned()`/`cast_signed()`, `f64::round_from(n)` and
`f32::round_from(x)` (nearest, ties to even), and `i64::try_from(f.trunc())?` (errors on NaN,
infinity, out of range). round_from and float TryFrom are provisional names. Rust's coherence rules
forbid implementing core's `TryFrom<f64> for i64`, or an inherent `f64::round_from`, outside core,
so the mechanism needs a recorded decision. Part of epic fx-yg5 (E1-P13).

## Scope

The replacements above in production std and the allowlist. cast_signed/cast_unsigned are Rust's
stable inherent methods: admit them. Research how each other spelling can resolve (for example
prelude traits, or a changed provisional spelling), decide, and record the decision on this bead
and, if a spelling changes, in design/01-design.md and design/reference.md §4.2 within the
reference's 25,000-token budget (a design edit goes through GOVERNANCE.md's review). FX0301 itself
is fx-u65's. No other new language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply.

## Acceptance

At the boundaries, truncate keeps the low bits; round_from ties to even; float-to-integer try_from
fails on NaN, both infinities, and out-of-range values; the documented spellings compile and run
through tide-admit with the production std. Toolchain tests prove each item executes. Std API
changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence.

title: std::arena (Arena, Id) and the #[pure] attribute
description:
## Why

design/reference.md §3.6 teaches `Arena<T>` with `Id<T>` handles for graphs and cycles: new,
insert(T) -> Id<T>, get, get_mut, remove, get_disjoint_mut, len, Index/IndexMut (panic on a stale
id), Default, contains, ...; §12.3 puts them at std::arena; §6.6 counts Arena as Pure when its
parts are. §6.6: `#[pure]` on a function makes losing authority-freedom FX0511, and E1 task B7's
reference uses it. Production std has neither. Part of epic fx-yg5 (E1-P13).

## Scope

std::arena::{Arena, Id} with §3.6's API, matching the conformance stub (conformance/rustc/std,
`pub mod arena`); `#[pure]` as a prelude attribute in tide-macros that the driver's existing FX0511
check (crates/tide-admit/src/pure.rs) reads; allowlist entries. FX0511's rule stays with its current
owner. No new language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply.

## Acceptance

A graph with a cycle built through Arena and Id runs; a stale Id panics on index; a `#[pure]`
function that reaches a capability fails with FX0511 and an authority-free one compiles and runs,
through tide-admit with the production std. Toolchain tests prove each item executes. Std API
changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence.
close_reason: Landed: std::arena and #[pure]. Codex r1 approve, Opus r2 text-only fixes, r3 rebase re-check approve. Landing suites on e0c6f07: workspace 261/0, conformance 297/12 AWAITS/0 FAIL, harness 69 OK, E1 references 28 pass (B7 now passes).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-yg5/report.md; the report lands in research/ as 25-casts-arena-allowlist.md with fx-yg5.3, the first of the three to land; the others cite it): adopt the report's §2 recommendations.
1. Arena<T>: Vec<Slot<T>> (generation + value or next-free), free-list head, live count; last-freed-first reuse (deterministic); a slot whose generation reaches u32::MAX is retired, never reused, so a stale Id never becomes valid again; insert panics past u32::MAX slots; get_disjoint_mut validates generations then uses slice::get_disjoint_mut (repeated id -> None); no unsafe. No cross-arena detection (design silent; a global counter would be ambient state); document it. iter order is slot order, not insertion order after reuse (document; reference marks iter provisional).
2. Id<T>: u32 index + u32 generation; hand-written Clone/Copy/PartialEq/Eq/Hash/PartialOrd/Ord/Debug with no T bound; PhantomData<fn() -> T>; Ord by index then generation. The stub's arena module becomes the shared production file.
3. Pure: Arena<T> is Pure exactly when T is (no change); Id<T> gets a pure.rs table entry making it Pure for every T (PURE-1's std table, versioned with std; not an FX0511 rule change). Conformance pins Id<Fs>: Pure accepted and Arena<Fs>: Pure rejected.
4. #[pure]: move the identity attribute from conformance/rustc/macros into tide-macros, export from the shared prelude in root.rs (one definition); tokens returned unchanged so spans survive; compile_error! for a non-function target or non-empty args. #[trusted_pure] is out of scope (reported).
5. Proof per the report §2.5: 02 §10.9's cyclic graph executes through tide-admit; stale index panics, get(stale) is None; #[pure] fn compiles and runs, one taking &Fs fails FX0511; the afree_pure_* cases still pass.

title: Task limits, deadlines, checkpoints, and isolation
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P1, and no existing bead owns it.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P1, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §7.1-7.2; design/03-authority-concurrency.md TASK rules and §9.3`

## Scope

Tasks::limit, Scope::set_deadline, Scope::cancel (unless fx-nkv.3 ships it), Tasks::checkpoint
(returning fx-o8j's std::task::Cancelled), Tasks::shield, Tasks::spawn_isolated and Panicked,
TaskError::DeadlineExceeded, on the thread runtime and under the seeded scheduler, and the global
deadlock report (03 §9.3) for tasks blocked waiting on a limit slot, sharing one report with
fx-o4h's channel waits. Production std under crates/, built and admitted through tide-admit; no new
language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply.

## Acceptance

A limited scope never runs more children than its limit and spawn waits as a checkpoint; a passed
scope deadline cancels and reports DeadlineExceeded or partial Ok results as 7.2 states; checkpoint
is level-triggered; spawn_isolated returns Err(Panicked) for a panicking closure without failing its
caller; a simulated run whose tasks all wait on limit slots reports a deadlock. Toolchain tests
prove each item executes, not only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the
production library owns runtime behavior.
close_reason: Landed 61453d7: Tasks::limit, scope deadlines, checkpoint, shield, spawn_isolated/Panicked, one runtime wait primitive and the deadlock report for limit waits; Codex r1, Opus r2-r3 approve; workspace 205, conformance 287/12/0.

Running an E1 reference to confirm this bead's surface no longer fails is allowed. A breach is recorded on fx-ic2 and needs a fresh held-out task set.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-time/report.md §§1.5-1.9, §4; see fx-o8j's comment of the same date): adopt the report's recommendations.
1. Deadlines: ScopeState.deadline: Option<Instant>, Cause::Deadline(scope); set_deadline stores min(old, t) and cancels at once if t <= now; reuse Runtime::cancel's first-cause propagation; an Err outcome after the scope's own deadline cause becomes Outcome::Deadline -> E::from(TaskError::DeadlineExceeded); nested scopes inheriting an ancestor's deadline report their children's own errors; set_deadline, cancel and shield are not scheduling points. Real side: deadlines detected lazily at checkpoints and bound blocking waits (soft deadlines; a late wake reports Cancelled, §4 item 10, record in 03).
2. One wait primitive (the single owner of blocking, AP-OWNERSHIP-001): wait(kind, span, until, cancellable) in the runtime; real side parks the thread in a loop that rechecks its condition, with the Thread handle registered so both cancel and the resource unpark it; sim side is a scheduler block with an optional class-1 timer. fx-o4h and fx-hxw add wait kinds only. Whichever of fx-o8j/fx-zc1 lands first builds it.
3. Tasks::limit: Tasks holds a chain of Arc<Limit> (n, live count, FIFO tickets) in derivation order; limited spawn: panic on a zero count; cancel check (cancelled -> not-started Task); take a slot in every count or none and queue a ticket in each (never hold one while waiting for another, §6.1); wait cancellable (shield hides outer causes, TASK-6); re-check on wake (pass the slot on if cancelled); then register, start, ordinary spawn point. Slots released in run() with the task-finish point. FIFO with direct hand-off (§4 item 6).
4. spawn_isolated: a real new task via thread::Builder, f under run()'s catch_unwind (baton hand-off outside destructors), caller's Context cloned in (checkpoints see the caller's scopes and set its echo bit), caller waits cancellable: false with wait isolated(task); Panicked.message = &str/String payload else fixed 'Box<dyn Any>'; process panic hook untouched; thread-creation failure panics in the caller.
5. Deadlock report: built by whichever of fx-zc1/fx-o4h lands first; lists every blocked task with wait kind and span; trace events per the report's §1.9 table.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Note (2026-11-11, from fx-o8j round-1 Opus review finding 3): fx-o8j's scheduler stores timers as BTreeMap<TimerKey, TaskId>, treats every fired key as a blocked task's timer, and counts a stall whenever any timer is pending. For class-0 scope deadlines: count only class-1 (operation) timers in the stall guard, so a CPU-only scope under a far deadline gets no false stall report; and the virtual-time advance has to reach Runtime (through Baton::pass), so that a deadline cancels and wakes waiters before any task runs. Lock order: runtime then resource (see fx-o4h); Limit lives in Tasks across Runtimes, so its release must wake its own waiters.

title: List resource handles in 02's not-Pure table
description:

title: Record build-cache, linker and agent-checkout prior art in research/03 and research/13
description:
## Why

The owner approved this on 2026-11-09 ('yeah'). The eon-efficiency research agent forwarded build-speed finds that Tide's research doesn't cover yet. They are prior art for D18's content-addressed artifact cache and for E4's edit-to-tests target (under 1 s), and recording them now saves a re-search when the incremental front end and E4 are scheduled.

## Scope

Docs-only. For each find, verify it against its primary source, then add a cited entry: what it is, the measured or claimed numbers with their source, and what it implies for Tide. Add each one to REFERENCES.md as well.
- mbx, Mr. Boxington (https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington; benchmarks https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/benchmarks; limits https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/limits): caches by normalized inputs, restores via hardlink or reflink, dedupes in-flight compiles, and runs a machine-wide scheduler. Reported: six parallel jobs went from 1m7s to 54.7s, with 31 peak rustc processes instead of 172. Goes in research/03 (cache prior art) and research/13 (fleet scheduling).
- kache (https://docs.rs/crate/kache): a zero-copy, content-addressed RUSTC_WRAPPER cache. Goes in research/03.

title: Settle seal mechanism gaps: phase, stable IDs, erased clauses, writer, manifest owner
description:
## Why

fx-koo planned the implementation of SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 (`design/04-contracts.md` §11.1),
the v0 seal check that fx-gcs waits on. Five points the code needs are unstated or
loose in the design, and each implementation slice would otherwise decide them alone,
giving several owners for one invariant (AP-OWNERSHIP-001). Settle them in their
owning documents first. These are technical choices; decide them (AGENTS.md, Decisions).

## Evidence

1. Where the check runs. `design/04-contracts.md:1319-1320` (SEAL-3) and
   `design/01-design.md:743` say the driver checks the seal "before rustc runs", but
   SEAL-2 (`04:1265-1274`) hashes what paths, method calls, operators, and
   projections resolve to, and counts an impl as applying "where the driver's trait
   selection cannot rule an impl out", which needs rustc's resolution and type
   analysis. D18 (`01:978-992`) already reads "before rustc runs" as before the crate
   is admitted, with checks before and after rustc's analysis. State which phase
   computes seal hashes and that nothing is emitted or run before FX0920 is decided.
2. Stable IDs. D14 (`01:894`) says "symbols have stable IDs"; SEAL-1 lists entries
   "by stable ID", and §11 (`04:1207`) and SEAL-2 resolve names "to stable IDs and
   content hashes" so a rename leaves a hash unchanged. Nothing defines a v0 stable
   ID, how hashed text abstracts the names it references, or how cycles (mutually
   recursive functions, recursive types) hash. The identity must extend, not
   duplicate, the public-item identity fx-kw8.10 and fx-kw8.11 introduce.
3. Erased clauses. Release builds erase clauses (`04:634-637`), but SEAL-2 computes a
   seal hash per configuration "after cfg evaluation", release included, and an
   interface entry fixes the contract. Say what a release-configuration hash covers.
4. The writer. SEAL-1 (`04:1247-1264`) has `tide seal` write `tide.seal`, but v0's
   toolchain is the `tide-admit` driver called by a trusted build caller, with no
   `tide` CLI yet (README "Status"). Name v0's writer and the provisional file format,
   so the corpus and the check share one.
5. The manifest. The manifest entry fixes grants, dependency grants, authority
   policies (D17, v0), and the `[contracts]` table. `tide.toml` is provisional
   (`design/reference.md:1022`), and grants reach the driver only as operator flags
   (`crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs:96-102`). Name the one owner that reads the
   manifest and passes its content to the check.

## Scope

In scope: `design/04-contracts.md` §11.1 (and §11 if stable IDs land there),
`design/01-design.md` D11, D14, or D18 where a point belongs there,
`conformance/rules.md` SEAL rows if they change, and `design/reference.md` only if the
core states something that changes (within 25,000 tokens, `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).

Out of scope: code; new seal semantics beyond what SEAL-1..6 state; SEAL-4 and SEAL-5
(`tide review`, FX0921).

## Acceptance

- Each of the five points is decided with reasons in its owning document, with no
  change to what a seal fixes (SEAL-2's covered parts stay as written).
- The decisions name one owner each for stable identity, clause normalization, seal
  file format, and manifest reading, matching fx-kw8.15 (identity), fx-kw8.16 (clauses), fx-kw8.17 (seal file), and fx-kw8.20 (manifest).

## Verification

- Review rounds under `GOVERNANCE.md` (docs-only design work: Opus review plus the
  Codex pass).
- `scripts/count-tokens.sh` if `design/reference.md` changes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a point cannot be settled without changing what a seal fixes; that is a
  scope call for the owner.

Codex draft report (2026-11-07, gpt-6.1-sol xhigh, research mode, worktree .worktrees/fx-zr3; Opus to decide):

## State

Research draft for fx-zr3 at `d12d7e00e970ac3395cd45690360f081062342fa`, 2026-11-07. No decision adopted; no tracked file, bead, branch, or commit changed. Opus must assess the identity metadata cost before closing this bead.

## Draft edits

Proposed replacements, conditional on Opus's decision:

- **Phase:** `design/01-design.md:743`, `design/04-contracts.md:1320,1423`, and the SEAL-3 inventory row: before, “before rustc runs”; after, “after rustc analysis, before artifact emission or execution”. At `01:978`, replace “before rustc runs” with “before artifact emission or execution”. Append to SEAL-3:

  > The driver computes hashes in `after_analysis`, using rustc's resolved and typed definitions. Earlier compiler errors reject the crate without a seal verdict. No metadata, interface artifact, executable, successful cache entry, or test process precedes successful seal checking. Compile-time evaluation remains subject to RUN-1.

- **Identity:** `01:894`, before: “symbols have stable IDs.” After:

  > The driver's identity owner (fx-kw8.15) extends the interface artifact's identity to private declarations, methods, and tests. Package-scoped opaque IDs persist in `// tide-id: ID` declaration comments; the writer provisions missing IDs before sealing, and renames preserve them. Duplicates in one configuration fail. Generated declarations derive IDs from their source owner's ID and semantic role. Names and rustc's numeric IDs are lookup data. References encode persistent IDs; local and generic binders encode positions. Hash a length-delimited, ID-sorted finite graph of covered definition parts and reference edges with SHA-256, visiting each node once; cycles require no recursive hash fixed point. Keep literals and semantic attributes, excluding formatting, documentation, and declaration-name spelling. Explicitly sealed paths remain fixed.

  At `04:1207`, replace “Names resolve to the content hashes of D14” with “The driver uses D14's identity and graph-hashing owner”. Distinct IDs remain distinct even for identical definitions; recomputed content, never an ID alone, establishes equality.

- **Erasure:** `04:634`, before: “Release builds erase clauses and ghost code.” After:

  > Release builds erase executable checks and ghost code. The driver's clause normalizer (fx-kw8.16) retains original clauses and typed, nonexecuting witnesses under the release configuration's cfg, before lowering erases them. Release hashes cover the same clause and dependency parts as debug hashes; cfg may select different definitions. Unresolvable clauses reject the build. Generated checking scaffolding is excluded from user-body hashes.

- **Writer:** `04:1250`, before: “`tide seal <path>..` adds entries”; after:

  > In architecture A, `tide-admit --tide-seal SOURCE --seal-entry PATH` adds entries; repeat `--seal-entry`. The existing `--whole`, `--manifest`, `--target`, and `--remove` meanings apply. The driver owns the provisional strict JSON format `tide-seal/1`: targets; entries with ID, path, kind; target/profile records with named part hashes and normalized clause records. Hashes are SHA-256. Reject duplicate/unknown fields and unsupported versions. Write identity metadata and the seal only after validating all requested configurations. A future `tide seal` delegates to this owner (fx-kw8.17).

- **Manifest:** append at D18's invocation paragraph (`01:996`) and cite from `04:1311`:

  > The driver owns manifest parsing (fx-kw8.20), snapshots `tide.toml` once, rejects malformed/unknown input, and supplies one parsed value to grants, policies, contract normalization, and manifest hashing. With a manifest, requested grants must fit the trusted caller's authorization ceiling; excess requests fail. Without one, direct-source invocations retain operator grants. Candidate manifests never select toolchain artifacts or compiler flags. Snapshot manifest, seal, identity metadata, and authorization inputs into cache keys before lookup.

- **Reference §0:** before: “You know Rust. Write Rust. A Tide program is a valid Rust 2024 crate: Tide's checker admits it, then a pinned nightly rustc builds it against Tide's std (D18).” After:

  > Write Rust 2024 against Tide's std (D18). Preserve `// tide-id: ...` comments on declarations when renaming; they carry stable identities.

Full proposed fixture files for fx-g2z; its future runner supplies the multi-file envelope. Each variant's `tide.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "test/seal"
version = "0.0.0"
```

`base/src/lib.rs`:

```rust
// tide-id: f
#[ensures(ok(result))]
pub fn f() -> u8 { 1 }
// tide-id: p
fn ok(x: u8) -> bool { x > 0 }
```

`rename/src/lib.rs`:

```rust
// tide-id: f
#[ensures(valid(result))]
pub fn f() -> u8 { 2 }
// tide-id: p
fn valid(x: u8) -> bool { x > 0 }
```

`changed/src/lib.rs`:

```rust
// tide-id: f
#[ensures(ok(result))]
pub fn f() -> u8 { 1 }
// tide-id: p
fn ok(x: u8) -> bool { x >= 0 }
```

Seal `crate::f` from base; copy that seal into each candidate. Check debug/test/release: rename accepts, changed reports FX0920/contract. Writer-generated hashes avoid stale fixtures.

Future driver patch sketch, not this bead's implementation:

```diff
 // invocation.rs: before cache lookup
+snapshot_manifest_seal_and_ids(); validate_requested_grants();
 // after_analysis, before interface::write
+let graph = identity::covered_graph(tcx, clauses::normalized(tcx));
+seal::check(&graph)?; // failure stops emission and cache promotion
```

## Checks run

- `br --no-db show`: fx-zr3, planning predecessor, implementation epic/prerequisites and dependents; exit 0.
- Pinned `rustc 1.99.0-nightly (771916f90)`: probe build initially failed twice (API/linker setup), then exited 0. Two recursive-crate analyses exited 0; helper rename changed DefPathHash. Injected `after_analysis` rejection exited 1 with zero output files. Release `if cfg!` unresolved-name probe exited 1/E0425; `#[cfg]` counterpart exited 0.
- Python finite-closure probe: exit 0, eight assertions, including cycles, rename, retargeting identical definitions, and unrelated edits.
- `conformance/run.sh --trace`: exit 0; SEAL-2/3 each have zero cases.
- `git diff --exit-code`: exit 0. Token measurements pending.

## Decisions for Opus

1. **Phase:** recommend one post-analysis gate. A separate analysis preflight also works but duplicates invocations/snapshot coordination. Pre-rustc checking needs a second resolver. Existing callback: `invocation.rs:60`; [pinned rustc ordering](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/771916f9028e7fe56d2685f2c4f698de5d7d6a45/compiler/rustc_driver_impl/src/lib.rs). Corpus needs rejection-without-output coverage; trust remains with rustc plus driver.
2. **Identity/cycles:** recommend persistent declaration IDs plus finite closure hashing. Sidecar IDs avoid source comments but require rename-map synchronization; source attributes add macro plumbing. Path IDs fail renames; content-only IDs conflate distinct definitions, so neither preserves SEAL-2. SCC hashing is a viable optimization with the same coverage. [Rust stable paths](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/queries/incremental-compilation-in-detail.html), [Unison's separate unique identity](https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/language-reference/unique-types/). Extend `interface.rs:50,86` and `interface/diff.rs:6`, version their schema; test recursion, duplication, moves, retargeting. IDs confer no approval.
3. **Erasure:** recommend retained witnesses; a separate same-cfg analysis build also works but costs another compile. Token-only hashing loses selected impls. `spikes/d18/macros/src/lib.rs:6` already retains release type checking. Add release predicate-edit coverage; preserve SEAL-2's trust boundary.
4. **Writer:** recommend driver mode/shared strict JSON. A thin CLI or separate executable sharing this owner works but adds packaging. Corpus calls the writer; it never blesses a candidate against the protected base (SEAL-4 unchanged).
5. **Manifest:** recommend driver parsing. A trusted caller parsing into a versioned typed input also works, at an extra protocol boundary. Source-selected grants alone breach README's operator-input boundary. Test excess grants, malformed input, and cache invalidation. No option needs to change SEAL-2's covered parts. All budget effects are confined to the reference replacement above; mechanics stay in 01/04.

## Open problems / next steps

Opus must accept or replace identity provisioning, including its source-writing workflow; name-only snapshots cannot establish persistent nominal identity. Then apply text, complete the fixture envelope under fx-g2z, and run governance reviews. fx-zr3 remains open.

Not run: full suites or Opus design review. Risk: draft identity provisioning remains unimplemented and unapproved.

comments.text:
Opus decision (2026-11-07, claude-opus-5-5):

# fx-zr3 decision (Opus, 2026-11-07, base d12d7e0)

Scratch file. Never commit it.

Evidence I checked myself: 04 §2.6, §11, §11.1 (SEAL-1..6 and the worked
example); 01 D11, D14, D18; conformance/rules.md SEAL rows; reference.md
§0 and §11; companion §18; research/06 ("content addressing as a derived
compiler index", text stays canonical); reviews/round43 and round44 (B2:
SEAL-2 leaves a named type's path free; "hash compared whatever the ID");
`crates/tide-admit/src/{interface.rs,interface/diff.rs,crates.rs,invocation.rs}`;
the beads fx-kw8.10, .15, .16, .17, .20, fx-g2z, fx-mhd; README "Status".

## Decision

### 1. Phase

The driver computes and checks seal hashes in its `after_analysis`
callback, after rustc's analysis and before rustc emits anything. Until
the check passes, nothing of the crate runs except compile-time evaluation
(RUN-1), and no metadata, trust artifact, executable, or cache entry is
written. A crate whose analysis fails gets no seal verdict; it is rejected
either way. `tide.seal` is snapshotted with the sources and is part of the
cache key.

Why: SEAL-2 hashes what paths, calls, operators, and projections resolve
to, and asks for trait selection. Only rustc's analysis has that. The
driver already writes the trust artifact in `after_analysis`
(`invocation.rs:60-70`) and stages output so that only successes are
promoted (`invocation.rs:736-812`). "Nothing is built or runs" therefore
holds without any new mechanism. D18 already runs checks both before and
after rustc's analysis, so "before rustc runs" was wrong wording, not a
second design.

Rejected:
- A pre-rustc check would need a second resolver, which is exactly what
  architecture A rules out.
- A separate analysis-only preflight run doubles the invocations and the
  snapshot coordination and buys nothing.

### 2. Stable IDs, name abstraction, cycles

v0 stable ID: an item's **path and kind**, which is the key that
fx-kw8.10's trust artifact already gives public items (`crates.key` plus
`def_descr`; `diff.rs:6` says "an item is its path and kind"). It extends
to private items, impl members by qualified path (`<Entry as
PartialEq>::eq`), and tests. A package's ID is its name (the manifest
entry, SEAL-4). Renaming or moving an item gives it a new ID.

Hashing (one owner: the driver's identity and hash module, fx-kw8.15):
- It reads rustc's resolved, typed definitions after `cfg`.
- It walks depth first from the hashed item. Each crate item reached is
  encoded once, where it is first met, and every later reference cites
  that visit position. So cycles need no fixed point, and two
  identical-content items stay distinct.
- Generic and local binders are positions.
- Referenced items' names are not hashed. The names a definition declares
  for its own parts are hashed: fields, variants, the items of a trait, and
  the members of an impl hashed in full.
- A std item is its path plus the toolchain version. A dependency item is
  its path plus the locked content hash.
- Sets with no source order (the impls that apply to a type) are sorted by
  their own hashes, so moving code between files changes nothing.

Rename versus replacement (SEAL-2): content hashing alone cannot tell
`fn lookup(id: UserId)` from `fn lookup(id: OrderId)` when the two newtypes
are identical, yet SEAL-2 says replacing a named item changes the hash. So
a crate item that the hashed text names counts as *renamed* only when both
of these hold:
- its old path resolves to no other item in the candidate;
- its new ID named no item at seal time.

The seal records the IDs this comparison needs. One cost follows:
renaming an item and reusing its old name in the same change reads as a
replacement (a conservative FX0920). I accept that.

Why: every v0 consumer can work with path IDs. A sealed item's own path is
already fixed by its entry. References to items that are not sealed are
name-abstracted. Approvals treat a renamed public item as removed plus
added, which is what `--tide-diff` already does. This extends fx-kw8.10's
identity and does not add a second one, as the bead requires. It also
follows research/06: text stays canonical and content addressing is a
derived index.

Rejected:
- **Persistent IDs in source (`// tide-id:` comments, Codex's
  recommendation).**
  - The writer would have to rewrite source across the crate, and every
    edit would have to keep the comments.
  - Copying a function duplicates its ID, and duplicate IDs fail the
    build. That is a new error, which the bead puts out of scope.
  - Agents would need new reference text, and the budget is already over
    (see Corrections).
  - The memo itself splits identity into two kinds ("ordinary unsealed
    artifacts can retain path/kind IDs until provisioned"). That
    duplicates fx-kw8.10's identity.
  - It buys no tamper resistance: a delegate can move the comments just as
    it can edit `tide.seal`.
- **Sidecar ID maps.** An honest rename leaves the map stale, so it fails
  SEAL-2's "renaming does not change it" unless rename detection is added.
  That detection is the rule above, without the map.
- **rustc's `DefPathHash`.** It changes on a rename (Codex's probe).
- **Content-only identity.** It merges identical nominal types (the
  UserId/OrderId hole).
- **SCC (strongly connected component) hashing.** Positional citation
  already handles cycles.

### 3. Erased clauses in release

Release erases clause evaluation, not the clauses. A release build still
resolves and type-checks every clause without evaluating it, as the body's
names resolve (CLAUSE-2). So a release seal hash covers exactly the
contract parts a debug hash covers, under the release `cfg`. A consequence
of CLAUSE-2: a clause cannot name an item that the release configuration
leaves out. Clauses enter hashes in normalized form, through the driver's
one clause normalizer (fx-kw8.16), never as the checks the contract macros
generate from them.

Why: a seal fixes a contract, not whether it runs. The D18 spike's macros
already lower clauses as `if cfg!(debug_assertions)`, which type-checks
them in release (`spikes/d18/macros/src/lib.rs:6`). This puts a
constraint on fx-mhd: its "erased in release" must keep a form that is
type-checked but never evaluated, and must not drop the tokens.

Rejected:
- A release hash without clauses: an item that exists only in release
  would have an unsealed contract.
- Hashing release clauses by tokens only: SEAL-2's resolution would be
  lost.
- A separate debug-`cfg` analysis to hash release: an extra compile, and
  it hashes the wrong `cfg`.

### 4. Writer and file format

Until a `tide` CLI exists, v0's writer is **the admission driver itself**,
in a seal mode. It takes the build's operator inputs plus SEAL-1's flags,
hashes each configuration it seals, and writes the file atomically, only
when every one of those configurations admits.

The driver owns the format: provisional JSON with a version tag
(`tide-seal/1`), like `tide-interface/1`. It contains:
- the sealed targets;
- for each entry, its stable ID and entry kind (interface, whole, or
  manifest), and, for each target and configuration:
  - a hash for each part SEAL-3 names;
  - each clause's kind, hash, and text, so that SEAL-3 can print a removed
    clause and label it `weakened`;
  - the IDs the rename rule compares.

The check reads only this format. Conformance cases take their seals from
the writer and never commit hash bytes (fx-g2z note 1). `tide seal` will
call the same owner (fx-kw8.17). The flag spelling, the hash algorithm,
and the field names are fx-kw8.17's to choose, and README records them.

Why: only the driver has the resolution the hashes need. Using JSON with a
format tag reuses the driver's existing hand-written artifact pattern and
adds no dependency. The file is only ever written by the machine.

Rejected:
- A separate binary or thin CLI: extra packaging, and the hashing would
  still live in the driver.
- TOML: no reader exists, and the manifest parser is a different owner.
- The corpus writing seal files itself: a second writer.

### 5. Manifest owner

**The driver is the one reader of `tide.toml`** (fx-kw8.20):
- It snapshots the manifest with the sources, so the manifest's bytes are
  part of the cache key.
- It rejects malformed input and unknown keys.
- It gives every consumer the same parsed content. The consumers include
  the grant check, the seal's manifest entry, and later policies and
  `[contracts]`.

The package's grants are the manifest's grants, and each one must be a
grant the trusted build caller passed. The caller's grants are a ceiling,
so candidate source never grants itself authority (README "Status").
Without a manifest, the caller's grants apply as they do today.

Why: the seal check runs in the driver and needs the whole manifest,
including policies and `[contracts]`, which no flag carries. A single
reader avoids a second serialization boundary. The ceiling keeps the
operator-input guarantee that README states.

Rejected:
- Manifest grants replacing the operator flags outright: the candidate
  could grant itself authority, which breaks README's boundary.
- The trusted caller parsing the manifest and passing typed input: a
  second protocol and a parser outside the repo for candidate-controlled
  bytes.
- Flags as the only grant source: the manifest's grants would have no
  effect, and the manifest would contradict the build.

The worked example still holds when the caller's ceiling includes `unsafe`.
When and how a grant above the ceiling is reported, relative to the seal
verdict, is fx-kw8.20's choice and is left unspecified here.

## Implementation instructions for Codex

Edit only these three files: `design/01-design.md`,
`design/04-contracts.md`, `conformance/rules.md`. Do not touch
`design/reference.md`, the companion, any fixtures (fx-g2z owns them), or
any code. Rewrap edited paragraphs to the width of the surrounding text
(01 bullets: two-space continuation indent, about 78 columns; 04: the same
as its neighbours). Keep the house style: present tense, no "now", no
"new".

### design/01-design.md

1. D11, sealed-delegation bullet (about lines 742-744).
   - Before: `The admission driver (D18) rejects a crate whose sealed item differs from its entry, before rustc runs; `tide review` and ...`
   - After: `The admission driver (D18) rejects a crate whose sealed item differs from its entry before rustc emits anything for it; `tide review` and ...`
2. D14, last bullet (lines 893-894).
   - Before: `Definitions are content-hashed; symbols have stable IDs.`
   - After: `Definitions are content-hashed; symbols have stable IDs. In v0 an item's ID is its path and kind (04 §11), which serves every v0 consumer: a sealed item's path is fixed anyway, and hashes leave out the names of the items they reference. Rejected for v0: IDs written into source, which every edit must keep and copying an item duplicates, and which a delegate can move anyway.`
3. D18, line 978.
   - Before: `- **Tide's checker gates every crate before rustc runs.**`
   - After: `- **Tide's checker gates every crate before rustc emits anything for it.**`
4. D18, architecture A (lines 991-992).
   - Before: `It checks resolved uses before rustc's analysis, and after it a backstop checks the instances that can run (03 ADMIT-1).`
   - After: `It checks resolved uses before rustc's analysis; after it, a backstop checks the instances that can run (03 ADMIT-1), and the seal check compares the crate with its `tide.seal` (04 SEAL-3).`
5. D18, "The driver owns every rustc invocation" bullet. Insert after `... keeps its own content-addressed cache instead of Cargo's build directory.` and before `A generated `Cargo.toml` ...`:
   - `It is the one reader of the package's `tide.toml`: it snapshots the manifest with the sources, so its bytes are part of the cache key, rejects malformed input and unknown keys, and gives every consumer the same parsed content, the grant check and the seal's manifest entry (04 §11.1) among them. The package's grants are the manifest's, and each must be one the trusted build caller passed, so candidate source never grants itself authority; without a manifest, the caller's grants apply.`

### design/04-contracts.md

6. §2.6, first sentence (line 636).
   - Before: `Release builds erase clauses and ghost code. The manifest can keep checks`
   - After: `Release builds erase clauses and ghost code: none of it runs or is compiled into the program. They still resolve and type-check each clause, as the body's names resolve (CLAUSE-2), so a release seal hash covers the same contract parts as a debug one (§11.1), and a clause cannot name an item the release configuration leaves out. The manifest can keep checks`
7. §11 "What is hashed" (lines 1207-1209).
   - Before: `Names resolve to the content hashes of D14, so a rename leaves the hash unchanged, while an edit to `spec fn is_sorted`, or to an ordinary `fn covers` that a `requires` calls, changes it.`
   - After:
     `Hashes read definitions after `cfg` evaluation, with rustc's resolution and types, and leave out the names of the items they reference, so a rename leaves the hash unchanged, while an edit to `spec fn is_sorted`, or to an ordinary `fn covers` that a `requires` calls, changes it. Clauses enter normalized, never as the checks the contract macros generate from them. In v0 an item's stable ID (D14) is its path and kind, as the trust artifact keys a public item (03 §4.1), for private items, impl members by qualified path, and tests too; a package's is its name. Renaming or moving an item gives it a new ID. The driver has one owner of these IDs and hashes, and one clause normalizer built on it. A hash walks depth first from its item, encodes each crate item it reaches once, where first met, and cites it by that position afterwards, so mutual recursion and recursive types need no fixed point, and two identical items it reaches stay two. Generic and local binders are positions. The names a definition gives its own parts, such as fields, variants, and the items of a trait or of an impl hashed in full, are hashed. A std item is its path under the toolchain version, a dependency's item its path under the locked content hash. Sets with no source order, such as the impls that apply to a type, go in the order of their own hashes, so moving code between files changes nothing.`
   - Keep the following sentence (`Proofs and `proof fn` bodies are excluded, ...`) unchanged.
8. SEAL-1, end (line 1264).
   - Before: `already pins. (File name and flags provisional.)`
   - After: `already pins. (File name and flags provisional.) Until a `tide` CLI exists, the admission driver (D18) is the writer, since only it has the resolution the hashes need: a seal mode that takes the build's operator inputs and these flags, hashes each configuration it seals, and writes the file atomically, only when every one of them admits. The driver owns the format, provisional JSON tagged with its version (`tide-seal/1`) as its trust artifact is: the sealed targets, and per entry its stable ID and entry kind (interface, whole, or manifest) with, per target and configuration, a hash for each part SEAL-3 names, each clause's kind, hash, and text, and the IDs SEAL-2's rename rule compares. The check reads only this format, conformance cases take their seals from the writer, and `tide seal` will call the same owner.`
9. SEAL-2, first paragraph. Insert before `Doc comments and formatting are not hashed.` (line 1273):
   - `A crate item the hashed text names counts as renamed, not replaced, only when its old path resolves to no other item in the candidate and its new ID named no item at seal time; the seal records the IDs this compares, so renaming an item and reusing its old name in one change reads as a replacement.`
10. SEAL-3, first sentence (lines 1319-1321).
    - Before: `The admission driver (D18) checks each crate against its own `tide.seal` before rustc runs, in each configuration it builds.`
    - After: `The admission driver (D18) checks each crate against its own `tide.seal` in each configuration it builds, after rustc's analysis, whose resolution and types the hashes need, and before rustc emits anything for the crate: until the check passes, nothing of the crate runs but compile-time evaluation (03 RUN-1), and no metadata, trust artifact, executable, or cache entry is written. A crate whose analysis fails is rejected with no seal verdict. The driver snapshots `tide.seal` with the sources, so its bytes are part of the cache key.`
    - Keep `An entry is checked in the configurations ...` and everything after it unchanged.
11. Worked example (lines 1422-1423).
    - Before: `Its `tide check` fails before rustc runs:`
    - After: `Its `tide check` fails before anything builds:` (the wording companion §18 uses).

### conformance/rules.md

12. SEAL-3 row (line 136). Replace `Before rustc runs, the driver checks the crate against its own `tide.seal`;` with `After rustc's analysis and before anything is emitted, the driver checks the crate against its own `tide.seal`;`. Leave the rest of the row as it is.
13. Line references. After edits 6-11, set each SEAL reference to the line where its bullet starts:
    - the SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 rows (lines 135-136);
    - the SEAL-1, SEAL-4, SEAL-5, and SEAL-6 entries in "Considered and excluded" (lines 185-188).

    Find the lines with `grep -n '\*\*SEAL-[1-6]\.' design/04-contracts.md`. They are stale already (SEAL-1 is cited as 04:1241 but sits at 04:1247). No other file cites 04 line numbers past 640; I checked with grep.

### Checks

- `conformance/run.sh` must exit 0, because rules.md changes.
- `grep -rn 'rustc runs' design conformance` must find no seal or gate sentence. Remember that the D11 phrase was wrapped across two lines, so grep for `rustc$` near "before" as well.
- `git diff --stat` must list only the three files above.
- `git diff --exit-code design/reference.md` must exit 0. No token count is needed because the file does not change. For the record, the base count is 25,019 (see Corrections).
- Then the GOVERNANCE review round for docs-only design work: an Opus review plus a Codex pass on the frozen candidate.
- Record on fx-zr3, in a comment, the owner map that the acceptance names:
  - identity and definition hashes: fx-kw8.15;
  - clause normalizer: fx-kw8.16;
  - seal writer and format: fx-kw8.17;
  - manifest reader and grant ceiling: fx-kw8.20.

  Also record decision 3's constraint on fx-mhd: release lowering keeps clauses type-checked and never evaluated.

## Corrections to the memo

1. **The identity design is replaced.** Dropped:
   - `// tide-id:` comments and writer-provisioned source IDs;
   - "duplicates fail" and generated-ID derivation, which are new
     diagnostics and new rules, out of scope;
   - "provisioned IDs throughout its closure; ordinary unsealed artifacts
     can retain path/kind IDs", which is two identities;
   - the "ID-sorted" graph, which needs persistent IDs. Visit-order
     positions do the same job without them.
2. **The reference §0 rewrite is dropped.** The memo rewrote the core
   reference's opening ("You know Rust. Write Rust.") to teach `tide-id`
   comments. That is unneeded and outside the bead's scope. Under this
   decision `reference.md` does not change.
3. **Token count.** `scripts/count-tokens.sh design/reference.md` gives
   **25,019** at base d12d7e0, measured twice with the same result. The
   reference is already 19 tokens over D14's 25,000 budget. This is
   pre-existing, so fx-zr3 does not touch it; it is reported as an
   out-of-scope finding. The memo called the count "pending" and
   "unverified".
4. **Writer.** The drafted `tide-admit --tide-seal SOURCE --seal-entry
   PATH` repeats the source entry, which is already the driver's
   positional argument. SHA-256, "strict JSON" field lists, and per-flag
   spellings are format details for fx-kw8.17 and do not belong in the
   design text. "Identity metadata" in the writer and cache-key text does
   not exist under this decision.
5. **Erasure.** "Unresolvable clauses reject the build" was drafted as a
   new rule. It is a consequence of CLAUSE-2 and is stated that way.
   "Typed, nonexecuting witnesses" is replaced by plain wording.
6. **Manifest.** "Candidate manifests never select toolchain artifacts or
   compiler flags" repeats RUN-2, so it is omitted.
7. **Fixtures.** The fx-g2z fixtures belong to fx-g2z, so they are not
   applied here. They also assume `tide-id` comments.

## Owner scope calls

None. All five points are mechanism choices for how the driver delivers
SEAL-1..6. The covered parts of SEAL-2 do not change. The one behavioural
edge is decision 2's rename-plus-reuse reading as a replacement. It is
conservative: it rejects a change that SEAL-2 would allow and never admits
one that SEAL-2 forbids. Decision 5's grant ceiling keeps an existing
README guarantee and adds no new one.

Out-of-scope finding for the caller: `design/reference.md` is at 25,019
tokens on main (d12d7e0), over the 25,000 budget that D14 says CI counts.
It needs a trimming bead, or a fix in whichever bead last grew it
(fx-kw8.23 edited it in db225c5).

Codex final fix report (2026-11-07):

## State

R3-B1 is fixed without committing, on `ffec143bea957f39b865b142c8c0372c5615d94a`. Tracked changes are limited to `design/04-contracts.md` and the six line citations in `conformance/rules.md`. All four review files remain untouched. The model and Rust probes are ignored scratch under `target/`.

Candidate diff SHA-256: `902db94cb5d665aeed2ba7031587f782c3494d650c6b912f6fd929f8a6a95f05`.

## Changes

- **Impl identity:** §11 defines an impl's path as its resolved qualified header, with kind `impl`. Trait arguments, positional type/lifetime/const binders (including const types), and canonical header predicates participate. Examples cover generic and blanket impls. These IDs use resolved names, not import spellings, source locations, body hashes or persistent annotations.
- **Inherent impls:** `<SELF>::{MEMBERS}` includes sorted declared member names/kinds, distinguishing multiple blocks with the same header. Rust permits multiple inherent blocks ([Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html)). Empty same-header blocks may share an ID; they retain separate graph nodes and table slots. When their colours also tie, they are interchangeable, so ordering them changes neither encoding nor the table.
- **Tie and rename behavior:** the residual tie rule uses these derived IDs. A trait/type rename changes the impl ID too. A/B/C still has no residual tie and accepts A-to-Z; without C, that rename reverses the header order and gives conservative FX0920. A referenced self-type rename can do the same. This qualifies name independence only at the existing residual tie-breaker; refinement remains name-independent.
- **Model:** `target/fx-zr3-r1/model.py` separates local integer node handles from derived stable IDs. Sorting, positional tables and inventories use `stable_id`; visited-node tracking uses handles. Renaming a trait/type automatically changes header IDs. Generic header codec checks consume resolved, positional terms, not Rust source. Duplicate-empty tests retain two equal IDs in distinct slots and detect an added third block.

## Checks run

- `timeout 30 python3 target/fx-zr3-r1/model.py`: **exit 0; 89 assertions**. Covers real header IDs, six A/B/C orders, local-handle independence, trait/self-type renames that preserve or reverse order, generic/blanket/lifetime/const/inherent IDs, duplicate empty blocks, sharing/cycles and the previous checks. New header and const-binder assertions each failed before correction (expected exit 1).
- Pinned `rustc 1.99.0-nightly (771916f90)`, scratch metadata probes: **8 impls accepted, exit 0**; duplicate `get` rejected with **E0592, exit 1**, as expected. No workspace build was run for these single-file probes.
- Read-only mechanism check: no concrete blocker; the checker independently ran the 89-assertion model. This is not governance approval.
- `git diff --check`: exit 0. Protected-file diff: exit 0; decision record, reference, companion, fixtures and production code unchanged. All six SEAL citations match; review-file hashes unchanged.
- Scope: **2 tracked files, 31 insertions / 12 deletions**.
- `bash /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/eon-overseer/heavy.sh conformance/run.sh` (closed stdin, bounded timeout, workspace-local TMPDIR): **exit 0; 194 PASS, 24 AWAITS CHECKER, 0 FAIL; 218 total**.

Not checked: production identity implementation or production-scale performance. Risk: residual-tie rename rejection remains intentional; governance confirmation remains pending.
